practical_context.visa: No visa required for French nationals (tourist stay up to 90 days). Valid passport required.
practical_context.currency: Japanese Yen (JPY). Credit cards widely accepted except at small shops and markets. Bring cash; ATMs at 7-Eleven stores.
practical_context.health: No mandatory vaccinations. Tap water safe to drink. High heat and humidity May–September—sunscreen and hydration essential. Jellyfish (habu kurage) June–October at beaches.
practical_context.transport: Rental car essential on the main island (no trains except Naha's Yui Rail monorail). International driving permit required. Frequent domestic flights between Naha, Ishigaki, and Miyakojima (ANA, JTA, Peach). Drive on the left.

itineraries.title: Grand Japan Rail Journey: Tokyo to Fukuoka by Shinkansen
itineraries.subtitle: Three weeks from Tokyo to Fukuoka aboard the bullet train, through ancient temples, sacred forests, and steaming bowls of ramen
itineraries.notes: Itinerary designed for the Japan Rail Pass (21 days). Long-distance transfers are via Shinkansen. Book your JR Pass before departure. In Kyoto and Osaka, use local buses and metro.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May (cherry blossoms) and October-November (fall foliage), temperatures 15-25°C. Avoid June-July (tsuyu rainy season, continuous rainfall, oppressive humidity) and July-August (stifling heat, possible typhoons). Spring and fall offer ideal conditions for train travel across the country.

visits.text: Sensō-ji is Tokyo's oldest temple—founded in 628 after two fishermen legendarily pulled a Kannon statue from their nets in the Sumida River. You'll first pass through Kaminarimon, the Thunder Gate, recognizable by its massive 700 kg red lantern guarded by the gods of wind and thunder. Beyond it, Nakamise-dōri stretches for 200 meters—one of Tokyo's oldest shopping streets, active since the Edo period. Arrive before 8:30 am: after 10 am, you'll feel the weight of 30 million annual visitors. Don't miss drawing an omikuji fortune—if it's bad luck, tie the paper strip to the designated racks.

Climb to the top floor of the Asakusa tourist information center, right across from Kaminarimon—the view of the temple and Skytree is free. Continue to the Sumida riverbanks to board at Azumabashi Bridge. The cruise to Hinode Pier takes about 40 minutes and passes under 13 bridges. You'll glide past Tokyo Skytree (634 meters, opened in 2012), the futuristic Asahi headquarters, and Hama-Rikyū Gardens. If you can, board just before sunset—the light on the Sumida is magnificent.

activities.text: In the evening, return to Asakusa for a twilight photo walk. Sensō-ji lit up at night has a different atmosphere—red lanterns glow in the dusk and the crowds have vanished. Push on to the Sumida River Walk, the pedestrian bridge attached to the Tobu railway bridge, for an unobstructed view of the illuminated Skytree.

visits.text: Akihabara, nicknamed "Electric Town," was born from the postwar black market when students resold radios cobbled together from military surplus. Today the district packs multi-story arcades, figurine shops, manga stores, and retro game boutiques. Exit through the Electric Town Exit of JR station. On Chūō-dōri, the main artery, the street is closed to cars on Sunday afternoons. If you like digging, dive into the side streets where independent shops hide the best finds.

Five minutes from Akihabara, don't miss Kanda Myōjin shrine, founded in 730. It hosts the Kanda Matsuri every two years, one of Tokyo's three greatest festivals. You'll see votive tablets illustrated with anime characters—a quintessentially Akihabara blend of tradition and pop culture.

Ginza is the district born in 1612 on the site of the former Mint—"ginza" means "seat of silver." After an 1872 fire, the Meiji government rebuilt it with brick buildings and Parisian-style boulevards. Stroll down Chūō-dōri, where luxury brand facades compete in audacity—Hermès in glass blocks, Mikimoto by Toyo Ito. In front of the Wako clock tower (former Seiko headquarters), note that in the 1954 Godzilla film, the monster reduces it to rubble when the clock strikes.

Step through the doors of Kabuki-za, Ginza's kabuki theater, open since 1889. Even without attending a full performance, you can buy a single-act ticket—an accessible way to discover this dramatic art without committing four hours.

activities.text: In the evening, treat yourself to a karaoke session in a private booth in Ginza or Shimbashi. The rooms are immaculate, often equipped with tambourines, and the catalog offers thousands of songs in multiple languages. Plan for one to two hours.

Head to Tsukiji Outer Market (the inner market moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the outer stalls remain). It's the perfect place to taste ultra-fresh sushi, tamagoyaki (sweet-savory omelets), and grilled tuna skewers. Arrive hungry.

visits.text: Takeshita-dōri in Harajuku is a 400-meter pedestrian avenue where Japanese street fashion expresses itself without filter—cosplay, lolita, streetwear. The street is narrow and packed on weekends. Pass through on a weekday morning if you want to circulate. You'll find stuffed crepes, kawaii boutiques, and multi-story sock shops.

Yoyogi Park, one of Tokyo's largest green spaces, transforms on weekends into an open-air stage: musicians, rockabilly dancers, cosplayers. On weekdays, it's calmer—perfect for catching your breath after Harajuku's effervescence. In spring, cherry blossoms draw crowds for hanami.

From Yoyogi, walk five minutes to Meiji-jingū shrine, dedicated to Emperor Meiji (died 1912) and Empress Shōken. Built in 1920, destroyed in 1945, and rebuilt in 1958 in cedar wood, it's nestled in a 70-hectare forest planted with 100,000 trees from across Japan. As soon as you pass under the 12-meter wooden torii, the city noise vanishes. It's the most visited shrine at New Year's—over 3 million worshippers. Curious detail: facing the sake barrels, you'll see wine casks from Burgundy, symbolizing openness to the West during the Meiji era.

Finish at Shibuya Crossing, the world's busiest pedestrian intersection—about 2,500 people cross at each green light, up to 3,000 during rush hour. Five crossings including one diagonal. To see it from above, climb to Shibuya Sky (230 meters, atop Scramble Square completed in 2019). Before crossing, stop at the Hachikō statue, the Akita dog who waited for his deceased master at the station for nine years (1925-1935). The current statue dates from 1948—the first, unveiled in 1934 with the dog himself present, was melted down during the war.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a break at one of Harajuku or Shibuya's theme cafés—cat cafés, hedgehog cafés, owl cafés, or anime-themed cafés. Each café has its own rules (duration, mandatory drink), but the experience is worth it. Plan for about an hour.

visits.text: Shimokitazawa—"Shimokita" to regulars—is Tokyo's bohemian quarter, three minutes from Shibuya by train. A former writers' refuge in the 1920s, it's transformed into a vintage fashion haven. Its pedestrian alleys overflow with impeccably organized thrift stores, record shops, independent cafés, and over 15 small theaters. Don't go before 11 am—most shops are still closed. Afternoon and evening is when the neighborhood comes alive.

The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Shinjuku, designed by Kenzō Tange and completed in 1991, rises to 243 meters. Its design supposedly draws inspiration from Notre-Dame de Paris and a computer chip. Each twin tower houses a free observatory on the 45th floor, at 202 meters. On clear days, Mount Fuji stands out on the horizon. The north observatory stays open until 10 pm—go in late afternoon to watch Tokyo light up.

Midday, detour through Shinjuku Gyoen, one of Tokyo's most beautiful gardens—58 hectares combining French garden, English garden, and traditional Japanese garden. It's one of the best hanami spots in spring, with over 1,000 cherry trees.

activities.text: In the evening, plunge into Omoide Yokochō (Memory Lane), a maze of tiny izakayas under the train tracks at Shinjuku's west exit. These few-seat counter establishments serve yakitori, gyōza, and beer in a postwar Tokyo atmosphere—the place has barely changed since the 1950s.

visits.text: Day at Tokyo Disney Resort in Urayasu (Chiba), about 20 minutes on JR Keiyō from Tokyo Station to Maihama. Two parks to choose from: Tokyo Disneyland (classic, ideal with children) or Tokyo DisneySea (unique in the world, more adult, inspired by maritime myths). DisneySea is often considered the most beautiful Disney park—its Mediterranean port setting, central volcano, and thrilling attractions deserve a full day. Plan to arrive at opening—lines explode after 11 am.

activities.text: If the park offers late opening (check the calendar), stay for the nighttime show on the lagoon—water projections, fireworks, and special effects. Otherwise, swing by Ikspiari shopping center at the park exit for dinner and exclusive souvenirs.

visits.text: Day trip to Hakone from Shinjuku—take the Odakyu Romancecar (about 80 minutes) and get the Hakone Free Pass covering train, bus, boat, and ropeway. Lake Ashi, nestled in a caldera at 720 meters altitude, crosses by pirate ship in 30 minutes. On clear days, you'll see Mount Fuji reflecting in its waters. Disembark at Moto-Hakone to reach Hakone-jinja shrine, hidden in the forest—its Heiwa torii, erected in 1951 to celebrate the peace treaty, stands at the water's edge. Expect a bit of patience for the photo—there's often a queue.

Take the ropeway to Owakudani, a volcanic valley born from Mount Hakone's last eruption 3,000 years ago. The landscape is almost lunar—yellowish ground, sulfur fumaroles, gray rocks. This is where they cook the famous kuro-tamago, eggs whose shells blacken in contact with 80°C sulfurous water. Legend says eating one extends your life by seven years. If the volcano is calm, you'll also have a spectacular view of Mount Fuji from the station.

activities.text: If you have time before returning to Tokyo, detour to the Hakone Open-Air Museum, a contemporary sculpture park nestled in the hills, with a Picasso pavilion and an outdoor foot bath.

visits.text: Transfer Tokyo → Kyoto via Nozomi Shinkansen from Tokyo Station (about 2h15, 476 km). Sit on the right side (seat E) facing forward—on clear days, Mount Fuji appears between Shin-Yokohama and Shizuoka, about 40 minutes after departure. It's a brief moment—keep your eyes open.

Once settled in Kyoto, head to Nishiki Market, nicknamed "Kyoto's kitchen." This 400-meter covered arcade, active for over 400 years, lines up more than 100 stalls of fish, pickled vegetables (tsukemono), tofu, matcha tea, and skewers. Taste yuba (soy milk skin, local specialty), fresh mochi, and tako tamago (small octopus stuffed with quail egg). The market closes around 5 pm—don't arrive too late.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll through Ponto-chō, a narrow alley parallel to the Kamo River, lined with restaurants and bars, some with terraces over the water (yuka) in summer. The atmosphere is hushed—paper lanterns, wooden facades. If you glimpse a kimono-clad figure slipping between doors, it might be a maiko (apprentice geisha) heading to an engagement.

visits.text: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion) has gleamed amid its mirror pond since 1397, when shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built it as a retirement villa. Its upper two stories are entirely covered in gold leaf—the ground floor, in natural wood, remains sober. Each floor represents a different style: Heian palace, samurai house, Zen temple. On July 2, 1950, a monk set fire to the pavilion—this episode inspired Yukio Mishima's novel. The current building is a faithful 1955 reconstruction. Arrive at opening (9 am) to avoid tour buses.

Nijō Castle, built in 1603 for first shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu, served as his residence during Kyoto visits. Its "nightingale" floors (uguisubari) intentionally creak underfoot to alert against intruders. The sliding panel paintings of Ninomaru Palace, executed by the Kanō school, are sumptuous. The gardens surrounding the castle deserve a leisurely stroll. Allow 1.5 hours for everything.

Gion, the historic geisha district, is explored on foot along Hanamikōji street. Teahouses (ochaya) with wooden facades line up their bamboo blinds—this is where maiko and geiko practice their art. The best time to glimpse a maiko hurrying to an engagement: between 5:30 and 6:30 pm. Stay discreet—don't chase them for photos.

activities.text: Participate in a tea ceremony (chanoyu) at one of the traditional teahouses in the district. The ceremony lasts about 45 minutes—they'll explain the ritual gestures, the meaning of whisked matcha, and the choice of wagashi (confection) accompanying the tea. Book in advance, especially during high season.

visits.text: Kiyomizu-dera (Pure Water Temple), founded in 778, perches on Otowa Hill. Its wooden terrace, supported by 139 thirteen-meter pillars assembled without a single nail, overlooks the valley and offers a panoramic view of Kyoto. The Japanese expression "jumping from Kiyomizu-dera" (making a bold decision) comes from the belief that surviving the jump guaranteed wish fulfillment. UNESCO-listed since 1994. To reach it, climb the shopping lanes of Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka—they're photogenic but very crowded after 10 am.

Heian-jingū shrine, built in 1895 to commemorate the 1,100th anniversary of the capital's transfer to Kyoto, is a two-thirds scale reproduction of the Heian period imperial palace. Its 24-meter vermilion torii is one of Japan's largest. Behind the shrine, the garden (paid) harbors a pond crossed by a covered bridge and over 3,000 plants—the weeping cherry trees are spectacular in April.

Fushimi Inari Taisha, founded in 711, is the head shrine of Japan's 30,000 Inari shrines. What makes it unique: roughly 10,000 vermilion torii donated by businesses and individuals form a tunnel along 4 km of trails climbing to the summit of Mount Inari (233 m). The most famous section, Senbon Torii, is at the bottom—but the higher you climb, the fewer people. The full round trip takes about 2-3 hours. The shrine never closes—going early morning or at nightfall, when the lanterns light up, is the best option.

activities.text: Late in the day, wander around Yasaka-jinja shrine at the entrance to Gion. Its paper lanterns light up at dusk and the atmosphere becomes hushed. If you have energy, push on to Maruyama Park just behind—it's Kyoto's most popular hanami spot in spring, with a century-old weeping cherry tree illuminated at night.

visits.text: Arashiyama Bamboo Grove is one of Kyoto's most iconic images—a path several hundred meters long bordered by giant bamboo whose stalks crack and whistle in the wind. To enjoy it without crowds, be there before 8 am. The path is short (10-15 minute walk), but the atmosphere is striking. Exiting, push through the gate of Tenryū-ji temple, UNESCO-listed, whose Zen garden facing the Arashiyama mountains is a masterpiece by landscape architect Musō Soseki (14th century).

Iwatayama Monkey Park shelters a colony of free-roaming Japanese macaques. The ascent takes about 20 minutes—the slope is steep but the path well-maintained. At the top, monkeys roam freely around you (don't look them in the eye, don't show food). The view over Kyoto from the summit is one of the city's finest.

activities.text: Descend toward Togetsukyō Bridge (the bridge that crosses the moon), Arashiyama's emblem. From the Katsura riverbank, the view of the bridge with mountains as backdrop is superb, especially in autumn when maples redden. If you have time, rent a bike to explore the surroundings at your pace—Gio-ji temple and its moss gardens are 15 minutes by bike.

visits.text: Excursion to Nara (45 min by JR train from Kyoto or Osaka). Tōdai-ji, founded in 728, houses the Daibutsu—a 15-meter-tall, 500-ton bronze Buddha, the world's largest covered bronze Buddha. The building that houses it, Daibutsuden, is one of the planet's largest wooden structures (57 m wide, 50 m high), even though the current version (rebuilt in 1709) is 30% smaller than the original. At the building's rear, try sliding through the hole in a pillar—according to belief, those who succeed attain enlightenment.

Kasuga Taisha shrine, founded in 768, is recognizable by its 3,000 lanterns—2,000 stone ones along the pathways and 1,000 bronze ones suspended in the buildings. They're all lit only twice a year, during the Setsubun (February) and Obon (August) festivals. The moss-lined lantern path leading to the shrine through Kasugayama forest is one of Nara's most beautiful.

If you have energy, climb Mount Wakakusa (342 m), a dome-shaped grassy hill from which the view over Nara and its temples is panoramic. The ascent takes 30-40 minutes. Every January, the slopes are burned during the Yamayaki festival—an impressive fire spectacle.

activities.text: Stroll through Nara Park where over 1,200 deer (shika) roam freely. These cervids are considered divine messengers in Shinto tradition. You can buy shika-senbei (deer crackers) from park vendors—beware, the deer can be insistent when they see food.

visits.text: Dōtonbori is Osaka's beating heart—a canal bordered by giant neon signs including the famous Glico Man, that runner with arms raised who's been shining since 1935 (the current version is the sixth). The district is paradise for kuidaore—"eat till you drop," Osaka's culinary philosophy. Walk along the canal and on Ebisu Bridge to snap the classic photo with Glico Man in the background.

Osaka Castle (Osaka-jō), initially built in 1583 by Toyotomi Hideyoshi to unify Japan, has been destroyed and rebuilt several times. The current tower dates from 1931 (reinforced concrete) and houses a museum on Hideyoshi's history and the castle's siege battles. Climb to the 8th floor for a 360° city view. The castle park, with its moats and cherry trees, is a favorite picnic spot for Osakans.

activities.text: Impossible to leave Osaka without a food tour of its specialties. Okonomiyaki (savory pancake filled with cabbage, meat, and sauce), takoyaki (octopus balls crispy outside and melting inside), and kushikatsu (fried breaded skewers) are the must-tries. The Shinsekai district, with its Tsūtenkaku tower and kushikatsu restaurants, is a good spot for dinner in a popular, retro atmosphere.

visits.text: Minoh Park (Minoo), north of Osaka, offers an easy 2.7 km hike along a stream to Minoh Falls, a 33-meter waterfall surrounded by forest. The trail is flat and well-developed—count about 40 minutes to reach it. In autumn, flaming maples frame the falls—it's one of the region's best momiji (autumn leaves) spots. On the return, taste fried maple leaves (momiji tempura), a local specialty sold in shops along the path.

activities.text: In the afternoon, explore America-mura (American Village), Osaka's young, alternative district with its streetwear boutiques, record shops, and trendy cafés. Continue on Shinsaibashi-suji, a 600-meter covered shopping arcade mixing international brands and local boutiques. It's Osaka's longest shopping street.

visits.text: Day at Universal Studios Japan (USJ), Osaka's theme park. The Wizarding World zone, reproducing Hogsmeade village and Hogwarts castle with meticulous attention to detail, is the park's star. Other zones (Jurassic World, Super Nintendo World with its life-sized Mario sets, Minion Park) are also worth exploring. Plan to arrive before opening and buy tickets online in advance—on high-attendance days, the park may refuse entry.

activities.text: If the calendar permits, stay for the nighttime show or parade. Times vary by season—check USJ's website in advance. During Halloween and Christmas periods, special events transform the park.

visits.text: En route to Hiroshima, stop in Himeji (30 min by Shinkansen from Shin-Osaka). Himeji Castle, nicknamed the White Heron, is Japan's most beautiful medieval castle—a 46-meter keep completed in 1609, never destroyed by war or earthquakes. UNESCO-listed and a national treasure, it was restored between 2009 and 2015 to recover its dazzling whiteness. The interior is austere (wooden walls, steep stairs) but climb to the 6th floor for the view and to understand the ingenious defensive system—loopholes, machicolations, labyrinthine passages. Allow at least 1.5 hours.

Right next to the castle, Kōkō-en garden, laid out in 1992 on the former grounds of samurai residences, brings together nine themed gardens connected by beaten-earth pathways. It's a quiet place to breathe after the castle visit. You can have matcha at the teahouse overlooking the garden.

activities.text: If you have time before catching the Shinkansen to Hiroshima (40 min), take the cable car up Mount Shosha to visit Engyō-ji, a Buddhist temple complex founded in 966 and used as a setting in the film The Last Samurai. The surrounding forest is magnificent.

visits.text: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, renovated in 2019, traces with sobriety and unflinching honesty the events of August 6, 1945, when the atomic bomb destroyed 90% of the city in an instant. Victims' personal effects, testimonies, and models are deeply moving. Allow at least 1.5 hours—and prepare yourself emotionally.

The Genbaku Dome (A-Bomb Dome), the only building left standing near the hypocenter, has been preserved as-is as a memorial. It's the former Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall, designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel and completed in 1915. UNESCO-listed in 1996. The surrounding Peace Memorial Park, with its cenotaph, peace flame, and peace bell, should be visited in silence—it's a place of reflection.

activities.text: After this intense visit, rent a bike to explore central Hiroshima, rebuilt around its seven rivers. The city has a pleasant rhythm, calmer than the major metropolises. Detour through Hondōri district to taste Hiroshima okonomiyaki—different from Osaka's: here the layers (noodles, cabbage, egg, sauce) are stacked instead of mixed.

visits.text: Itsukushima Shrine, founded in 593 and rebuilt in its current form in 1168 by Taira no Kiyomori, seems to float on water at high tide. Its great 16-meter vermilion torii, planted in the sea 200 meters from shore, is one of Japan's symbols. At low tide, you can walk to the torii's base—check tide times before planning your visit. The entire shrine is UNESCO-listed.

Daishō-in temple, on the slopes of Mount Misen, is often overshadowed by Itsukushima but well worth the detour. It's the island's main Buddhist temple—its staircases lined with hundreds of copper prayer wheels, its statues covered with knitted caps, and its sea view are enchanting. Less crowded than the shrine, it offers a more intimate atmosphere.

activities.text: Ascending Mount Misen (535 m), Miyajima's highest point, can be done on foot (about 1.5 hours of sustained climbing) or by combining cable car and walk (20 min walk from the arrival station). At the summit, the view embraces the Seto Inland Sea and its dozens of islands. According to tradition, Kōbō Daishi (founder of Shingon Buddhism) lit a flame there 1,200 years ago—it supposedly still burns in one of the summit temples.

practical_info.duration: ~1.5h on foot or 30 min cable car + walk

visits.text: Transfer Miyajima → Fukuoka: ferry from Miyajima to Miyajimaguchi (10 min), then JR to Hiroshima (30 min), then Nozomi or Sakura Shinkansen to Hakata (about 1h). Allow 2 to 2.5 hours for the entire journey.

Tenjin is Fukuoka's main shopping district—underground shopping arcades (Tenjin Chika), department stores, and boutiques spread across several city blocks. Calmer and more spacious than Tokyo or Osaka shopping districts, it's a good place to wander and buy souvenirs.

activities.text: In the evening, head to the yatai of Nakasu—these street stalls set up along the Naka River and around Tenjin are a Fukuoka institution. You sit at the counter (6-8 seats maximum per yatai), order a bowl of Hakata ramen (milky pork broth, thin noodles), and chat with the cook and neighbors. Yatai open around 6 pm and close around 1 am. Arrive early to get a seat—they don't take reservations.

visits.text: Ohori Park, laid out around an artificial lake inspired by Hangzhou's West Lake in China, is Fukuoka's green lung. A 2 km promenade circles the lake—it's locals' favorite jogging circuit. The traditional Japanese garden (paid) on the south shore is an oasis of calm. Just next door, Fukuoka Castle ruins (Maizuru Park) offer a panoramic city view from the former stone terraces of the keep.

Canal City Hakata is a shopping and entertainment complex built around an artificial canal—fountains come alive every 30 minutes with a water and light show. The curved architecture by American Jon Jerde is spectacular. It's also a good eating spot: "Ramen Stadium" on the 5th floor brings together ramen restaurants from across Japan.

activities.text: Take advantage of your time in Fukuoka to taste different variants of Hakata ramen—creamy tonkotsu (pork bone) broth, ultra-thin noodles you can order extra-firm (kata-men or bari-kata). Most restaurants offer kaedama, an extra portion of noodles to add to your bowl to extend the pleasure.

visits.text: Excursion to Dazaifu (30 min by Nishitetsu train from Tenjin). Dazaifu Tenmangū shrine, founded in 905, is dedicated to Sugawara no Michizane, deified as Tenjin, the kami of study and literature. Thousands of students come to pray before exams. In front of the shrine, the first plum blossom (ume) supposedly flew from Kyoto to follow its exiled master—the legend of the "flying plum." The access avenue is lined with shops selling umegae-mochi, rice cakes filled with red bean paste and stamped with a plum blossom.

Just behind the shrine, the Kyushu National Museum, designed by Kikkawa Kiyonori, is a massive glass and steel building nestled in the hill. It traces the history of cultural exchanges between Japan, China, and Korea. The architecture alone is worth the trip—the forest reflections on the curved facade are striking.

activities.text: Before catching the train back, stroll through Dazaifu's historic lanes. This small town was the seat of Kyushu's regional government in the 8th century—it has a tranquil pace and streets lined with traditional houses that contrast with Fukuoka's energy.

visits.text: Nanzōin temple in Sasaguri (20 min by JR from Hakata) houses one of the world's largest reclining bronze Buddhas—41 meters long, 11 meters high, 300 tons. Built in 1995, it's less ancient than its Southeast Asian rivals but its size impresses. The complex is nestled in forest and little frequented by tourists—it's a peaceful place to end your circuit. Take time to visit the 88 small shrines of the miniature Shikoku pilgrimage, scattered in the hills around the temple.

activities.text: Last afternoon in Japan—return to Hakata and Tenjin districts for final shopping. Department store basements (depachika) are the best place to buy boxes of Japanese confections to bring home. Hakata Tōrimon (white bean paste filled cakes) and mentaiko (marinated cod roe) are Fukuoka specialties not to miss.

seo.h1_title: Grand Japan Rail Journey: Tokyo to Fukuoka by Shinkansen
seo.intro_paragraph: Step into Tokyo's luminous districts, then slow down in Kyoto among gardens and alleyways. Savor Osaka's street food flavors, discover Hiroshima's quiet strength, approach Miyajima from the sea. End in Fukuoka amid the yatai atmosphere where ramen steam draws passersby. Three weeks aboard the Shinkansen, from temple to temple, bowl to bowl.
seo.seo_hook: Moss gardens, hilltop castles, ramen steam in night markets. Three weeks from Tokyo to Fukuoka to grasp Japan's depth, one Shinkansen at a time.
featured_list: Kyoto: a thousand vermilion torii at Fushimi Inari, tea ceremony in Gion
Osaka: steaming takoyaki in Dōtonbori, Hideyoshi's castle at twilight
Hiroshima: peace memorial and rebirth along seven rivers
Miyajima: Itsukushima's floating torii, Mount Misen ascent facing the Inland Sea
Fukuoka: Hakata ramen at yatai stalls, Nanzōin's reclining Buddha

highlights: 30 million annual visitors to Sensō-ji, Tokyo's oldest temple (628)
10,000 vermilion torii at Fushimi Inari, 4 km trail up Mount Inari
Himeji Castle, Japan's only never-destroyed medieval castle, UNESCO-listed
Itsukushima's floating torii on Miyajima, shrine founded in 593

itineraries.title: Grand Tour of Japan in 22 Days: Tokyo to Hiroshima
itineraries.subtitle: You cross Honshu from east to west chaining metropolises, UNESCO shrines, Japan Alps, and Hiroshima memories.
itineraries.notes: Kamikochi closes from November 15—check dates before booking. JR Pass doesn't cover Kamikochi/Takayama/Kanazawa buses. November offers autumn colors (momiji) but nights are cool at altitude.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May (cherry blossoms) and October-November (fall colors), temperatures 15-25°C. Avoid June-July (rainy season), July-August (oppressive heat and humidity, up to 35°C), and September (typhoon risk). Kamikochi closed November-April (snow).

visits.text: Step through the Kaminarimon Gate by 7:30 AM to see Senso-ji nearly empty. Founded in 628 after two fisherman brothers discovered a statue of Kannon in the Sumida River, it's Tokyo's oldest Buddhist temple. The giant red lantern at the entrance weighs about 700 kg. The current building dates from the 1950s—the March 1945 bombings destroyed everything except the residents' determination to rebuild it identically.

Walking toward Senso-ji, Nakamise-dori draws you in. This 250-meter shopping arcade lines up about 90 shops that have been selling souvenirs, fans, ningyo-yaki (small red bean cakes), and grilled senbei since the late 17th century. Just beside it, the covered Shin-Nakamise-dori continues with cafés, restaurants, and artisans. Try a warm melon pan or dango while strolling.

Head to Tokyo Skytree: at 634 meters, it's Japan's tallest tower and the world's second-tallest structure since its 2012 opening. Two observation decks at 350m and 450m. On clear days, you can spot Mount Fuji. Tickets cost around 2,100 ¥ for the first level. Book online the day before to skip 1-2 hour lines.

Ueno Park spans 53 hectares since opening in 1873—it's Japan's first public park. At its heart, Ueno Toshogu Shrine founded in 1627 is also dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu. This jewel covered in gold leaf survived major earthquakes and the 1945 bombings. The grounds also house a lantern gallery of 50 stone and bronze lanterns offered by daimyo lords.

activities.text: Explore Ameyoko, the market street running along the tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi. Its name comes from "Ameya Yokocho" (confectioners' alley) and evokes its post-war black market past. Today 400 stalls sell dried fish, exotic fruits, sneakers, and spices. It's one of the rare Tokyo spots where vendors shout their prices—a sonic shock after the city's polite silence.

Finish at a traditional izakaya in Asakusa's back streets. Order yakitori (grilled skewers), edamame, and an Asahi beer or warm sake. The vibe is unpretentious, prices reasonable (2,000 to 3,500 ¥ per person). One rule: shoes stay on but silence at the table is earned by the clink of glasses as you say "kanpai!"

visits.text: Meiji Jingu Shrine was inaugurated in 1920 to honor Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken. Bombed in 1945, it was rebuilt in 1958. The most striking feature is its forest: 100,000 trees donated from all over Japan and hand-planted, now grown into a mature 70-hectare forest in the heart of Tokyo. Pass through the great 12-meter cypress torii and let Harajuku's din disappear within steps.

Yoyogi Park adjoins the shrine, offering 54 hectares of lawns, ponds, and paths. Created in 1967 on the site of the 1964 Olympic Village, it's where Tokyoites picnic, rehearse choreography, or play guitar on Sundays. Walk through it to experience the city differently, far from crowded sidewalks.

Takeshita-dori—400 meters of packed sidewalk—concentrates kawaii fashion, giant crepes, gothic-lolita boutiques, and Japanese streetwear. Since the 1980s it's been the laboratory of Tokyo youth trends. Try a Marion crepe (strawberry-whipped cream) or Totti Candy Factory's rainbow cotton candy. Avoid Saturday afternoons when crowds become unbearable.

Shibuya Crossing sees up to 3,000 pedestrians per light cycle during rush hour—it's the world's busiest intersection. Three free or near-free viewpoints: 11th floor of Shibuya Hikarie (free), Starbucks Tsutaya facing the crossing (crowded), or Magnet by Shibuya 109 rooftop (about 1,800 ¥ with a drink). The Hachiko statue nearby honors the Akita dog who waited for his deceased master for 9 years until his own death in 1935.

activities.text: Dine in Omoide Yokocho in Shinjuku, the "memory lane" also nicknamed Piss Alley. These 60 tiny stalls (5-10 stools each) have served yakitori and ramen since the post-war era, in a smoky, convivial atmosphere. Budget 2,000 to 3,000 ¥. Continue with a stroll through Kabukicho, the red-light district: you can wander safely, but avoid touts offering "clubs"—tourist scams are common.

practical_info.tip: Never follow a tout outside Kabukicho, even to a supposedly cheaper bar

activities.text: To extend the evening, head up the Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Shinjuku. Two observatories at 202 meters, free entry until 10 PM. 360° views of the illuminated skyline and, on clear nights, Fuji's silhouette on the horizon. Less touristy than Skytree, and no lines.

visits.text: Yanaka is one of the rare Tokyo neighborhoods to have survived the great 1923 earthquake and 1945 bombings. Result: narrow alleys, period wooden houses, and a shitamachi (low city) atmosphere found nowhere else. Yanaka Ginza street, 170 meters lined with 70 small shops, remains run by families who've kept shop for three generations—fishmongers, tofu vendors, senbei makers.

Yanaka Cemetery spans 10 hectares and holds over 7,000 graves, including that of the last shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu. The central avenue lined with cherry trees becomes a pink tunnel in spring. In November, maples take over. It's a living cemetery: joggers, stray cats (Yanaka has hundreds), and residents cross it daily.

Nezu Shrine is one of Tokyo's oldest—founded nearly 1,900 years ago according to tradition, with current buildings dating from 1706 on orders of shogun Tsunayoshi. Its tunnel of miniature torii rivals Fushimi Inari in miniature. In late April, 3,000 azaleas of 100 varieties color the hillside. Entry is free—it's a well-kept secret.

Akihabara is the kingdom of electronics and otaku culture. The nickname "Electric Town" dates to the 1950s when the black market for radios and components exploded here. Today, entire buildings dedicated to manga, figurines, retro games, maid cafés. Yodobashi Camera Akiba on 9 floors remains a must-see even for non-geeks.

activities.text: Sample a taiyaki (fish-shaped waffle filled with red bean paste) at Yanaka Shippoya, one of the street's iconic shops. Or try matcha ice cream from Himitsudo, artisan since 1997. These tasting stops punctuate the walk and immerse you in local habits.

Step into a maid café in Akihabara for the experience—@home cafe is the most famous. The waitresses greet you shouting "okaerinasai goshujin-sama!" (welcome home, master). You eat decorated omurice, clap in rhythm. It's kitsch, unapologetic, and a fascinating window into an entire slice of Japanese pop culture. Budget 1,500 to 3,000 ¥.

practical_info.tip: Photos of staff forbidden without paid permission

visits.text: Nikko Toshogu is the mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the shogunate that ruled Japan for 250 years. Built in 1617 by his son Hidetada, then massively expanded in 1636 by his grandson Iemitsu, it brings together 55 buildings covered in gilding and carvings—completely atypical in a culture where Shinto simplicity dominates. The famous Nemuri Neko (sleeping cat) carving and the three monkeys "see no evil, speak no evil, hear no evil" are here. UNESCO-listed since 1999, entry 1,600 ¥.

Cross the Shinkyo, the vermillion "sacred bridge" spanning 28 meters over the Daiya River. Built in 1636, it was rebuilt identically in 1904 after a flood. Legend tells that priest Shodo Shonin managed to cross the river in the 8th century thanks to two divine serpents who served as a bridge. Paid access: 300 ¥.

Rinno-ji is Nikko's major Buddhist temple, founded in the 8th century by the same monk Shodo Shonin. The Sanbutsudo (Hall of Three Buddhas) houses three 8-meter-tall gilded statues. Just beside it, the Sanbutsu-ji path winds through centuries-old cedars to various shrines. Sanbutsudo entry costs 400 ¥.

Kegon Falls drops 97 meters—one of Japan's three most famous waterfalls. It forms the outlet of Lake Chuzenji and you can admire it from a free platform or from the lower observatory, accessible by elevator (570 ¥). In November, the cliff blazes with reds and golds.

activities.text: Circle Lake Chuzenji, formed 20,000 years ago by Mount Nantai's eruption. At 1,269 meters altitude, its shores take on extraordinary colors in November. Pleasure boat (1,400 ¥ round-trip) or hiking trail around the lake—allow 2-3 hours for a partial loop.

Taste yuba, Nikko's local specialty: it's the skin of soy milk, skimmed from the surface during tofu production. High in protein, unique texture, served as sashimi, in soup, or fried. Several restaurants in town make it their signature—try Hippari Dako or Meiji no Yakata (heritage addresses, about 2,500 ¥ for a set meal).

visits.text: Yudaki Falls pours 70 meters of water from Lake Yunoko. Less monumental than Kegon but wilder, cascading over volcanic rocks. Easy access from the Yudaki-iri bus stop. Its ochres and golds in November are unforgettable.

Senjogahara Marshland spans 400 hectares at 1,400 meters altitude, formed by the gradual drying of an ancient lake. A 2-km wooden walkway crosses this protected wetland. In November, golden grasses wave in the wind with Mount Nantai as backdrop. Twin marsh Odashirogahara nearby, more intimate.

Return train to Tokyo in late afternoon from Tobu-Nikko Station. The direct Revaty Kegon or Spacia takes 1h50. Enjoy the scenery rolling by: terraced rice paddies, traditional villages, then gradually the megalopolis densifying.

activities.text: Hike the trail linking Yudaki to Senjogahara: 4 km, 1h30, gentle elevation gain. It's Nikko National Park's most accessible hike, perfect for breathing fresh air before diving back into Tokyo. Dress warmly in November—temperatures drop quickly at altitude.

practical_info.tip: Bring water, no shops on the trail

activities.text: Before the train, treat yourself to an onsen (thermal bath) at Yumoto Onsen, historic hot spring at 1,500 meters altitude. The whitish sulfurous water soothes muscles after hiking. Public baths from 700 ¥.

visits.text: Lake Kawaguchi is one of five lakes surrounding Mount Fuji, formed 1,000 years ago by lava flows that dammed the valley. Its north shore offers the classic postcard view: Fuji reflecting in the water. On calm mornings, the symmetry is perfect (phenomenon called "sakasa Fuji"). The lake is 21 km in circumference and 14 meters maximum depth.

Oishi Park on the north shore is THE photo spot for Fuji. In season, lavender (June-July), red kochia (October-November), or cosmos create a colorful foreground. In November, red maples frame the volcano. Free entry. An on-site café serves matcha latte decorated in Fuji shape.

Mount Fuji stands at 3,776 meters—an active stratovolcano whose last eruption was in 1707. A sacred site in Shintoism, it's been UNESCO-listed since 2013 as an "object of artistic inspiration." From November to February, its summit remains snow-capped. Best viewing: morning (before 10 AM) to avoid afternoon clouds.

activities.text: Rent an electric bike at Sazanami (about 1,500 ¥ for 4h) and circle the lake: 20 km, 3 hours with photo stops. The circuit is flat and well-marked, alternating touristy south shore and wild north side. Multiple Fuji viewpoints—few hikes are this photogenic.

practical_info.tip: Leave early, Fuji often hides in the afternoon

activities.text: Take the Kachi Kachi ropeway (Mount Tenjo Ropeway) from the lake's east shore. In 3 minutes, you climb to 1,075 meters for stunning views of Fuji and the lake. Round-trip 1,000 ¥. The site tells the Kachi-Kachi Yama legend, a 19th-century Japanese tale. Walk down if you prefer (45-min path).

Taste hoto, Yamanashi Prefecture's specialty: thick soup of flat noodles in miso broth with pumpkin, leek, and mushrooms. Created to feed warriors of the Takeda clan in the 16th century. Hoto Fudo has 5 branches around the lake, budget 1,500 ¥.

visits.text: Chureito Pagoda is part of Arakura Sengen Shrine, built in 1958 in memory of Fujiyoshida soldiers fallen in war. But it's the viewpoint that made it famous: climb 398 steps and you overlook the five-story red pagoda with Mount Fuji behind. One of Japan's most shared photos. Free entry.

Matsumoto Castle is one of five Japanese castles classified as "National Treasure" and the country's oldest five-story, six-floor wooden keep. Built in the late 16th century (keep completed around 1594), it's the only flatland castle to have preserved its original wooden keep—others burned or were rebuilt in concrete. Nicknamed "Karasu-jo" (crow castle) for its black lacquered exterior. Entry 700 ¥.

Downtown Matsumoto has preserved its Edo charm in the Nakamachi and Nawate-dori districts. Nawate, nicknamed "frog street" (referencing the nearby river), lines up craft shops, street food stalls, and amphibian statues. Nakamachi is renowned for its white warehouses with black roofs, housing galleries and cafés.

activities.text: Take the Keio bus from Kawaguchiko to Matsumoto: about 3 hours, via the Japan Alps. The route crosses spectacular mountain landscapes, and toward Nagano you see snow-capped peaks appear. Book the day before (about 4,500 ¥).

practical_info.booking: Reservation required on Keio Bus or Highway Bus

activities.text: Enjoy a soba meal in Matsumoto. These buckwheat noodles are regional pride: the city and surroundings have produced renowned buckwheat since the Edo era. Try zaru soba (cold, dipped in dashi) at Kobayashi Soba—family address since 1910, about 1,500 ¥.

visits.text: Kappa Bridge (Kappa-bashi) is Kamikochi's emblem—a 36.6-meter wooden footbridge spanning the icy turquoise Azusa River. The Hotaka peaks (3,190 m) tower above. The kappa is an aquatic creature from Japanese folklore said to inhabit these waters. The current bridge dates from 1997, built identically to the 1927 model.

Taisho Pond formed in 1915 during Mount Yake's eruption, which dammed the Azusa River. Hence its name, marking the Taisho era. Dead tree trunks emerging from clear waters with the Alps as backdrop compose an almost ghostly landscape. 20 min walk from Kappa-bashi. Striking reflections in early hours.

Myojin Pond is a natural mirror nestled at the foot of Mount Myojin (2,931 m). Hotaka-jinja Okumiya shrine nearby is dedicated to the mountain god. Access on foot from Kappa-bashi: about 1h along the Azusa, flat and well-maintained trail. Entry 500 ¥ around the pond.

activities.text: Classic hike Kappa-bashi → Myojin → Taisho Pond: 15 km round-trip on flat trail along the Azusa River. Allow 4-5 hours with breaks. Wildlife to observe: Japanese macaques, snow monkeys, and with luck, rock ptarmigan. Protected area—stay on marked trails.

practical_info.tip: Kamikochi closes from November 15—check dates imperative

activities.text: Kamikochi access: local train from Matsumoto to Shin-Shimashima (30 min), then Alpico bus (60 min, about 2,450 ¥). Note that private cars have been banned in the valley since the 1970s to protect the site. JR Pass doesn't cover this segment.

visits.text: Takayama Jinya is the only Edo-era regional government building still standing in Japan. Built in 1615, it served as the shogunate's administrative headquarters for 176 years. Tatami mat rooms, period kitchens, prison, and interrogation room are open to visit. Every morning on the esplanade: Jinya-mae Asaichi market (local products, crafts). Entry 440 ¥.

Sanmachi-suji is Takayama's old merchant quarter. Three parallel streets preserved since the Edo era, with dark wooden houses, window grilles, and lanterns. Sake breweries are numerous—when you see a cedar ball (sugidama) hanging, there's fresh sake. Free tastings or 200-500 ¥.

Hida Folk Village brings together 30 traditional houses transported from surrounding mountain villages then reconstructed here. Some are over 500 years old, with their gassho-zukuri thatched roofs (hands folded in prayer). Entry 700 ¥. 10 min by bus from Takayama Station.

activities.text: Savor Hida beef, a wagyu breed raised locally for over 14 generations of selected cattle. Marbled fat, melts in the mouth. Several preparations: yakiniku (grilled at table), sushi (raw), korokke (croquette). Maison Kojima Ryori serves a lunch set for 3,000 ¥, dinner for 6,000 ¥.

Take the Higashiyama trail: 3.5 km, about 2 hours, connecting 15 temples and shrines on the city's eastern hills. Monks' favorite meditation path, with panoramic views over the old town. Ancient cedar forest, old cemeteries, few tourists.

visits.text: Kenrokuen is considered one of Japan's three most beautiful gardens along with Korakuen and Kairakuen. Designed over 11.4 hectares between the 17th and 19th centuries by the Maeda lords, its name means "garden of six qualities" (spacious, secluded, artificial, venerable, water-rich, panoramic). Its Karasaki maple is 170 years old. In November, yukitsuri (pyramidal rope supports) protect pines from snow weight. Entry 320 ¥.

Kanazawa Castle was the residence of the Maeda clan for nearly three centuries, from 1583 to 1868. Several fires ravaged it; the current reconstruction uses only traditional techniques—not a single nail. The Ishikawa-mon gate (1788) is original. Park entry free, 320 ¥ for main buildings.

Higashi Chaya was Kanazawa's largest geisha district since 1820. Three cobbled streets lined with red-façaded houses with kimusuko wooden lattices. Still active today: five geishas (geiko) practice here. Visit Shima house (500 ¥), opened to public since 2003, or Kaikaro which offers tea with maiko.

Nagamachi, the samurai district, preserves its yellow earthen walls (dobei) and narrow alleys. The Nomura house, high-ranking samurai of the Maeda clan, offers an intimate glimpse: tatami room, miniature garden with koi carp. Entry 550 ¥. In winter, walls are protected by straw mats (komomaki).

activities.text: Explore Omicho Market, "Kanazawa's kitchen" since 1721. 170 stalls: fishmongers, snow crabs (local specialty November-March), sea urchin, vegetables, takeout snacks. Try a kaisen-don (ultra-fresh sashimi rice bowl) for 2,000-3,000 ¥. Open 9 AM-5 PM.

Try Kanazawa's edible gold leaf, which produces 99% of Japan's leaf gold since the 16th century. Vanilla ice cream entirely covered in gold (Hakuichi, about 900 ¥) or golden matcha cake. There are also workshops for applying gold leaf to objects.

visits.text: The 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, nicknamed "Maru Bijutsukan" (the round museum), was designed by SANAA agency in 2004. Circular glass building with no back façade, inviting entry from all sides. Permanent installation "Swimming Pool" by Leandro Erlich creates the illusion of a traversable pool. Won Golden Lion at Venice Biennale. Free entry for open zones, 450 ¥ for exhibitions.

Myoryuji, nicknamed "ninja temple," is a Nichiren temple built in 1643 under cover of a Buddhist sanctuary—actually a disguised fortress for Maeda clan samurai. Seven apparent floors hide 23 rooms, 29 staircases, trapdoors, traps. Guided tour mandatory (in Japanese, French booklet provided). Phone reservation essential. 1,200 ¥.

Nishi Chaya, the third geisha district, is the smallest and most discreet. A single cobbled street, but still alive with active teahouses. Nishi Chayagai Museum (free) tells a geisha's daily life a century ago. Less touristy than Higashi Chaya.

activities.text: Try a gold leaf workshop at Hakuichi or Kanazawa Yasue-yunuki: apply a leaf yourself to a small lacquered box or pair of chopsticks. 1,500 to 3,500 ¥ depending on object. The artisan explains the process: gold is hammered here until reaching 0.0001 mm thickness.

Learn tea ceremony at Shima teahouse in Higashi Chaya, dating from 1820. A master guides you through ritual gestures: whisking matcha, serving, drinking in three sips. Service in kimono, accompanied by seasonal wagashi. About 1,500 ¥.

Oyama Shrine, built in 1873, honors Maeda Toshiie, clan founder. Its gate (Shinmon) surprises: designed in 1875 by a Dutch architect, it mixes Japanese, Chinese, and European styles, with a colorful stained-glass window at the top. Totally atypical in Japan.

visits.text: Nijo Castle was built in 1603 as the first shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu's official residence in Kyoto. UNESCO-listed since 1994. Its Ninomaru Palace impresses with "nightingale floors" (uguisubari) that sing at every step—revolutionary anti-ninja system. Paradoxically, this is where the last shogun Yoshinobu officially returned power to the emperor in 1867. Entry 1,300 ¥.

Nishiki Market, nicknamed "Kyoto's kitchen," stretches 400 meters over 5 blocks with 130 stalls. It has existed since the 1310s as a fish market. Today: fresh tofu, tsukemono (fermented vegetables), yuba, tamago-yaki (sweet omelets), sashimi, wagashi sweets. Free entry, but budget 1,500-2,500 ¥ for snacking.

To-ji Temple was founded in 796, just after Kyoto's founding. Its five-story pagoda stands 55 meters—Japan's tallest wooden structure. Destroyed several times, rebuilt in 1644. Entry 800 ¥ for main buildings. On the 21st of each month, Kobo-san flea market with 1,200 stalls.

Kyoto Tower, 131 meters high, was inaugurated in 1964. Its observatory at 100m offers complete city views and, on clear days, out to the Higashiyama and western mountains. Entry 900 ¥. Illuminated in white at night, it was long controversial for its modern look facing millennial temples.

activities.text: Sample snacks at Nishiki Market: tako-tamago (octopus with quail egg head, 500 ¥), fried tofu sticks, glazed soy, iced matcha tea. Some shops have existed over 400 years and deserve a look inside—Aritsugu for instance has forged knives since 1560.

In the Karasuma-Shijo-Kawaramachi district, Kyoto's commercial and nightlife heart, stroll covered Teramachi and Shinkyogoku galleries, then a light kaiseki dinner or obanzai (Kyoto home cooking) in one of Pontocho-dori's izakaya. 3,000-6,000 ¥.

visits.text: Fushimi Inari Taisha, founded in 711 by the Hata clan, is the head shrine of Inari deity (rice, fertility, commerce). About 10,000 vermillion torii form a tunnel climbing Mount Inari (233 m). Each gate was donated by a company or individual—current price: 175,000 to 1.3 million yen. Full loop: 2-3 hours. Open 24/7, free.

Kiyomizu-dera, founded in 778, is UNESCO-listed. Its main hall sits on a gigantic 13-meter-high wooden terrace without a single nail. 139 zelkova pillars support it. The expression "jump from Kiyomizu's veranda" (launch into something risky) comes from here: 234 people actually did it in the Edo era (85% survived). Entry 500 ¥.

Sannen-zaka and Ninen-zaka are two steep cobbled streets leading to Kiyomizu-dera. Built in the 8th century, preserved in their Edo state. Wooden façades, lanterns, and ceramic shops (Kiyomizu-yaki is local pottery). Legend says whoever stumbles on these pavements dies within 3 years—stay careful!

Yasaka Pagoda (Hokan-ji) towers over the district at 46 meters. Built in 1440, it's one of Kyoto's oldest standing pagodas. Photogenic anytime: framed by narrow alleys it creates the postcard silhouette of Gion. Its interior occasionally opens (400 ¥).

Gion is the geisha district since the 17th century. Its Hanamikoji and Shirakawa alleys preserve machiya (narrow, deep houses) and okiya (geisha houses). Still 80 geishas and maiko active. You might spot them around 6 PM, en route to a banquet—don't photograph them without asking.

activities.text: Discover Chion-in, headquarters of the Jodo school (Pure Land Buddhism), founded in 1234. Its 24-meter-high Sanmon gate is Japan's largest temple wooden gate (1621). Its 74-ton bell is struck 108 times every December 31st. Free entry, 300 ¥ for gardens.

Dine in Pontocho, a 500-meter cobbled alley parallel to the Kamo River. 100 restaurants of all ranges line up their red lanterns. The fanciest have a yuka: wooden terrace over the river (May-September). Budget 4,000-15,000 ¥ for kaiseki.

visits.text: Kinkaku-ji (officially Rokuon-ji), the Golden Pavilion, was built in 1397 as shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu's retirement villa, then converted to a Zen temple upon his death in 1408. The upper two floors are covered in pure gold leaf (0.5 μm thick). Burned by a monk in 1950 (Mishima's novel "The Golden Pavilion"), the current building dates from 1955. UNESCO since 1994. Entry 500 ¥.

A 10-minute walk away, Ryoan-ji houses Japan's most famous dry Zen garden (karesansui), created around 1500. Fifteen stones arranged on raked gravel, but only 14 visible simultaneously from any angle—only wisdom allows seeing them all. UNESCO-listed. Entry 600 ¥.

Tenryu-ji is Arashiyama's main Zen temple, founded in 1339 in memory of Emperor Go-Daigo. UNESCO-listed. Its Sogenchi garden, designed by monk Muso Soseki, has remained virtually unchanged for 700 years—one of Japan's first "strolling gardens" using Arashiyama's mountains as natural backdrop (shakkei). Garden entry 500 ¥.

Arashiyama's bamboo grove covers 16 hectares. Its stalks reach 20 meters. The sound of wind in the leaves was officially classified as "one of 100 soundscapes of Japan to preserve." Very touristy during the day—come before 9 AM or after 5 PM to experience the true atmosphere.

activities.text: Walk Togetsukyo bridge ("moon-crossing bridge"), 155 meters long over the Katsura River. Built in the 9th century, rebuilt several times, current version in wood-painted concrete dates from 1934. Arashiyama's photo meeting point, with mountains in background. Traditional yakatabune boats offer river rides (1,500 ¥, 30 min).

Stop at a tofu artisan in Arashiyama—the district is renowned for it. Sagano Yudofu Sanjuku offers boiled tofu (yudofu) served in several preparations, in a traditional building beside a garden. 3,800 ¥ for the set.

visits.text: Mount Kurama, north of Kyoto, is a sacred site linked to tengu (mythological creatures). Kurama-dera temple, founded in 770, nestles on the mountainside. Paved ascent path through ancient cedars, 1 hour climb. Perched sanctuary, valley views. Cosmic energy said to be particularly intense here according to shugendo.

Descend on foot to Kibune village—30 min hike. Kibune-jinja, founded 1,600 years ago, is dedicated to the water god. Its entrance stairway lined with red lanterns is iconic. In November, flaming maples compose an extraordinary setting. The village is famous for its kawadoko restaurants (terraces over the river, in summer).

Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion, was built in 1482 by shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa as a retreat, inspired by his grandfather's Golden Pavilion. The silver was never applied—project abandoned for lack of funds during the Onin War. Its white sand garden "sea of silver" (Ginshadan) with its "Kogetsudai" cone imitating Mount Fuji is unique. UNESCO. Entry 500 ¥.

Heian Shrine was built in 1895 for Kyoto's 1,100th anniversary. It reproduces at reduced scale (5/8) the original imperial palace of 794. Its vermillion-painted concrete torii at 24 meters is one of Japan's largest. Its 30,000 m² gardens (600 ¥) line up 1,000 cherry trees. The building is recent but the architectural feat is debated.

activities.text: Take the Philosopher's Path (Tetsugaku no Michi): 2 km along a canal lined with 450 cherry trees, connecting Ginkaku-ji to Nanzen-ji. Named because philosopher Nishida Kitaro walked it daily. In November, maples dominate. Several small temples en route (free Honen-in worth the detour).

Enjoy a shojin-ryori meal (Buddhist vegetarian cuisine) at Nanzen-ji or a nearby temple. Based on 5 colors, 5 flavors, 5 preparation methods—strictly vegan and codified since the 13th century. 3,000-8,000 ¥ for set meal. Reservation essential.

visits.text: Todai-ji houses the Daibutsu, a 15-meter-tall, 500-ton bronze Buddha statue cast in 752. Its Daibutsuden is the world's largest ancient wooden structure—even though rebuilt in 1709 at only two-thirds its original size. The pillar with a hole at the base: if you pass through (size of the Buddha's nostril), you're promised enlightenment. Entry 600 ¥.

Nara Park is home to 1,200 sika deer roaming freely. Considered divine messengers since the 8th century, they're protected by law—killing a deer was punished by death until 1637. You buy special crackers (shika senbei, 200 ¥) from approved vendors. Deer bow to get them—learned behavior by tradition.

Kasuga Taisha, founded in 768, is the Fujiwara clan's main shrine. Famous for its 3,000 stone lanterns lining the access path and 1,000 bronze lanterns suspended in the grounds. Illuminated twice yearly (February and August). The Man'yo secondary grounds are planted with 250 plants mentioned in the Manyoshu (8th-century poetic anthology). Free grounds entry, 500 ¥ for inner sanctuary.

Kofuku-ji was founded in 669. Its five-story pagoda stands 50 meters and dates from 1426—Japan's second-tallest. Its National Treasures Museum houses exceptional wooden Buddhist statues, including the three-faced, six-armed Ashura. UNESCO. Museum entry 700 ¥.

activities.text: Stroll Isuien Garden, a traditional landscape garden in two parts (17th and 19th centuries) using Mount Wakakusa and Todai-ji's gate as background ("shakkei" technique). Soba restaurant on-site. Entry 1,200 ¥. Its twin Yoshikien is free for foreigners.

Taste freshly pounded mochi at Nakatanidou: artisans pound glutinous rice with mochitsuki (huge wooden mallet) at spectacular speed, 150 strikes in two minutes. Yomogi (mugwort) ball stuffed with red bean paste, still warm. 200 ¥ piece, eat immediately.

visits.text: Osaka Castle was built by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1583, unifying Japan after a century of civil wars. The current keep is a 1931 concrete reconstruction furnished as a museum. Panoramic view from the 8th floor. The surrounding 106-hectare park is magnificent in November. Keep entry 600 ¥.

Dotonbori is Osaka's neon heart for 400 years. Its eponymous canal was dug in 1612. The Glico running man sign (1935, current 6th version) and the giant Kani Doraku crab are icons. It's the temple of kuidaore ("eat till you drop"): takoyaki, okonomiyaki, kushikatsu, fugu.

Shinsekai, "new world," was built in 1912 inspired by Paris (north) and New York (south). Its 103-meter Tsutenkaku Tower, rebuilt in 1956, dominates the district. Once a seedy area, now a popular neighborhood renowned for kushikatsu skewers. Quick visit but unique Osaka atmosphere.

activities.text: Try okonomiyaki, Osaka's iconic "Japanese pancake": batter of cabbage, egg, bacon, sauce, mayonnaise, bonito flakes dancing from the heat. At Mizuno in Dotonbori (since 1945) or Kiji, budget 1,200-2,000 ¥. The Hiroshima version is layered, Osaka version mixed—don't confuse them.

Explore Kuromon Market (600 meters, 150 shops since 1902), nicknamed "Osaka's kitchen." Grilled seafood on-site, Kobe beef sashimi, sea urchin, fresh wasabi. Budget 2,000-4,000 ¥ for a complete tasting. Open 9 AM-6 PM.

End the evening with a drink atop Umeda Sky Building, free observatory (entry 1,500 ¥) at 173 meters with floating walkway connecting two towers. Signature Hiroshi Hara architecture (1993). 360° views of nighttime Osaka, lights as far as the eye can see.

visits.text: The Genbaku Dome is the only building left standing near the hypocenter of the atomic bomb dropped on August 6, 1945 at 8:15 AM. Built in 1915 as the Industrial Promotion Hall, it stood 150 meters from the explosion's vertical point—the downward force spared its frame. UNESCO-listed in 1996. Preserved in its August 6th state. You can't enter, but walking around outside is deeply moving.

Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park was designed by Kenzo Tange and inaugurated in 1954. The central Cenotaph holds the names of all identified victims (now over 340,000). The Flame of Peace has burned since 1964 and won't be extinguished until all nuclear weapons are abolished. The Children's Monument honors Sadako Sasaki, who died of leukemia at 12 after folding over 1,000 origami cranes.

The Peace Memorial Museum is one of the world's most harrowing museums. It assembles victims' personal items, photos, testimonies. The east wing (2019 renovation) recounts August 6th minute by minute. No sensationalist images, but an emotional depth that marks you for life. Allow at least 2 hours. Entry 200 ¥.

Ferry across (10 min) to Miyajima, "island of gods." Itsukushima Shrine, founded in the 6th century, was built on stilts at the sea's edge because the entire island was considered too sacred to set foot on. At high tide, the 16-meter-tall floating torii (camphor wood, 60 tons) seems to drift. UNESCO since 1996. Entry 300 ¥.

activities.text: Osaka-Hiroshima journey: Shinkansen Sakura or Nozomi, 1h30, about 10,000 ¥ (covered by JR Pass except Nozomi). Numbered seats, wifi, perfect cleanliness.

Enjoy Miyajima's sacred deer, which roam freely like in Nara but are more discreet. Regular street walkers, they sometimes steal tourist maps from distracted visitors. Also taste the giant oysters (kaki), produced in the bay and island specialty—grilled with lemon, 400 ¥ each.

visits.text: Daisho-in is Miyajima's oldest temple, founded in 806 by Kukai, founder of Shingon Buddhism. The access stairway is lined with 500 rakan statues (Buddha's disciples), all different. Mantra prayer wheels to spin. Mystical atmosphere, much less crowded than Itsukushima. Free entry.

Mount Misen peaks at 535 meters and offers extraordinary panoramas of the Seto Inland Sea and its islands. Miyajima Ropeway from Momijidani, in two sections, 30 min journey (2,000 ¥ round-trip). At the summit, 30-min trail to the true peak with Reikado temple housing an "eternal flame" lit by Kukai 1,200 years ago.

Return to Hiroshima and castle visit. Built in 1589 by lord Mori Terumoto, completely destroyed by the 1945 atomic bomb. Rebuilt identically in 1958, it now houses a samurai history museum. Entry 370 ¥. Free park, pleasant for a late afternoon stroll.

Mitaki-dera, perched on Mount Mitaki's flanks in northwest Hiroshima, was founded in 809. Its name comes from the site's three waterfalls. Three-story pagoda transported here in 1951 from central Hiroshima to commemorate victims. Mossy forest path, rare oasis of peace in the city. Free.

activities.text: Try Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki: "layered" version with a thin crepe, cabbage, noodles (yakisoba or udon), egg, sauce. Created in the 1950s to feed the post-war population cheaply. Okonomi-mura brings together 25 counters on 4 floors. 1,000-1,500 ¥.
Return to Hiroshima by ferry + train from Miyajima (40 min total). Head to your hotel in the city center, near the station or Peace Park to simplify tomorrow.

visits.text: Shukkei-en, "miniature scenery garden," was created in 1620 by lord Asano. It miniaturizes 60 famous Chinese landscapes, notably West Lake in Hangzhou. Destroyed by the bomb in 1945, then rebuilt identically. 4 hectares, central pond, bridges, teahouses. Entry 260 ¥. Peaceful stroll before departure.

Hondori, a 500-meter covered shopping street in Hiroshima's heart, gathers nearly 200 shops and restaurants. Perfect for last-minute shopping or okonomiyaki before the train. Very local atmosphere, few tourists despite the size.

Hiroshima Station: catch Shinkansen Nozomi or Hikari to Tokyo. 4-5 hours depending on train, about 19,000 ¥. Cross Kansai, pass within kilometers of Mount Fuji on the north side. Last chance to see Japanese landscapes rolling by at 300 km/h.

activities.text: Final ekiben to buy at the station before the train. These regional lunch boxes are a tradition: each station offers its own. In Hiroshima: anaguni-meshi (grilled eel on rice), oysters, or lunchbox inspired by local baseball. 1,000-2,000 ¥. Perfect ritual before leaving the region.
Night in Tokyo, ideally in a hotel near the airport (Narita or Haneda depending on your flight). Pack, rest. Return flight scheduled tomorrow.

visits.text: Last Tokyo morning, adapt to flight time. If you have time, stop at Tokyo Station whose Marunouchi façade (1914) was restored in 2012 in its Belle Époque style. Two steps away, the Imperial Palace and its outer gardens (free) offer a final calm look at the capital.

Ginza shopping district for a last souvenir—high-end boutiques but also Uniqlo Ginza (12 floors!), Itoya for Japanese stationery, or Don Quijote for pop goodies. The main street is pedestrian on weekend afternoons.

Airport journey: from Tokyo Station, the Narita Express (N'EX) reaches Narita in 53 minutes (3,070 ¥). For Haneda, the monorail from Hamamatsucho in 13 minutes (500 ¥). Allow 3 hours before your flight for international checks.

activities.text: Final ramen bowl before leaving Japan. At Tokyo Station Ramen Street (basement, 8 master ramen shops) or in any neighborhood near your hotel. 900-1,500 ¥. Nostalgia guaranteed two weeks later.

At the airport, tax refund on purchases if you kept receipts (10% VAT refunded above 5,000 ¥ purchases in certain shops). Final round in duty-free shops: matcha KitKats in quantity, Tokyo cookies, sake, unique Japanese perfumes.

seo.h1_title: Grand Tour of Japan in 22 Days: Tokyo to Hiroshima
seo.intro_paragraph: Three weeks to cross Honshu from east to west: Tokyo the metropolis, Nikko and its golden mausoleums, Mount Fuji and the Japan Alps, Kanazawa the samurai city, Kyoto with 2,000 temples, Nara and its sacred deer, Hiroshima and Miyajima. A November itinerary combining autumn colors, UNESCO sites, regional gastronomy, and historical memory.
seo.seo_hook: Tokyo to Hiroshima: 22 days across Honshu, 10 prefectures, 5 UNESCO sites, golden temples, Japan Alps, and autumn colors.

Kawaguchiko: iconic view of Fuji (3,776m) and its Chureito Pagoda
