itineraries.title: Kyushu & Yakushima Circuit: Volcanoes and Ancient Forests
itineraries.subtitle: 13 days from Kitakyushu to Yakushima: feudal castles, mythological gorges, Beppu's smoking hells, Aso's volcanic crater, and Yakushima's UNESCO primeval forest
itineraries.notes: Mandatory ferry Kagoshima→Yakushima on the final day (2 hours by high-speed jetfoil) or domestic flight (35 min). Access to Aso crater subject to volcanic activity - check aso-volcano.jp before departure. Kawachi Fujien open only mid-April to mid-May (wisteria) and mid-November to early December (maples) - verify dates. Dazaifu Tenmangu: main hall under renovation until 2027, Sou Fujimoto's temporary pavilion open to visitors.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-May and October-November, temperatures 18-24°C. Avoid June-July (rainy season, monsoon), August-September (oppressive heat 30-33°C + typhoons). Yakushima is extremely rainy year-round, bring waterproof gear.

visits.text: The Mojiko Retro district is a walk through Meiji-era Japan without the artificial reconstruction. Moji Port opened in 1889 as an international trade hub, and its Western-style buildings survived - a rarity in Japan. Mojiko Station (1914), the first station in Japan designated an Important Cultural Property, sets the tone with its neo-renaissance facade. Two minutes on foot, the Mitsui Club (1921) is a half-timbered mansion built by Mitsui & Co. to host merchants and their clients: Albert Einstein stayed here in 1922, and the room he occupied remains in its original state. Wander down to the waterfront to see the Blue Wing Moji, a 108-meter pedestrian drawbridge that opens every hour to let boats pass - a spectacle in itself.

Kokura Castle has dominated the city since 1602, when Hosokawa Tadaoki had it built following the Battle of Sekigahara. The original structure burned in 1866 during inter-clan warfare, and the current keep - reconstructed in concrete in 1959 - adopts a karazukuri style where the top floor is larger than the one below, giving it its distinctive silhouette. From the top, 360° views over Kitakyushu. The park is lined with 300 cherry trees in spring. The small historical detail absent from most guides: in August 1945, Kokura was the primary target for the second atomic bomb. That morning, thick fog blanketed the city. After three unsuccessful passes, the B-29 diverted to its secondary target - Nagasaki.

activities.text: Mojiko's signature dish is yaki curry: rice and curry baked together in the oven with cheese until a golden, crispy crust forms. Every restaurant in the district has its own recipe. Expect a 30-minute wait on weekends. In winter (late November to mid-February), over 300,000 lights illuminate the historic buildings for Mojiko's Roman Illumination - one of Kyushu's most spectacular night displays.

From Mojiko Port, a small ferry crosses in 5 minutes to Karato Market in Shimonoseki (Honshu) - perfect for a fresh fugu (pufferfish) sashimi break, the city's specialty. An international crossing just steps from your overnight stay.

visits.text: Hidden in the forested hills south of Kitakyushu lies Kawachi Fujien, a private garden opened in 1977 by the Higuchi family. In 2015, CNN selected it among Japan's 31 most beautiful sites - and attendance exploded. The main attraction: two wisteria tunnels, one 80 meters and the other 110 meters long, under which violet, white, and pink cascades fall like curtains. The large pergola covers over 3,000 tsubo (roughly 10,000 sq ft) of trellis draped with 22 wisteria varieties. Peak viewing is late April to early May - advance online booking mandatory during peak season, tickets sell out fast. In autumn (mid-November to early December), maples take over.

activities.text: To reach the garden, take the train to Yahata Station, then Nishitetsu bus #56 to the Kamishigeta terminus (25 minutes). From the stop, it's about 45-55 minutes on foot - bring comfortable shoes. By car, the journey is much simpler (free parking). Outside the wisteria bloom peak, entry is free and the garden nearly empty: another way to discover it at your own pace.

practical_info.booking: Booking required during bloom season (mid-April to mid-May)
practical_info.season: Mid-April to mid-May (wisteria), mid-November to early December (maples)

visits.text: Dazaifu Tenmangu is Japan's largest Tenjin shrine - the kami of learning - and it's built directly over the grave of Sugawara no Michizane (845-903). Michizane was a brilliant scholar at the Heian imperial court, exiled to Dazaifu by the jealous Fujiwara clan. He died two years later, and disasters immediately struck the capital. The official interpretation: his vengeful spirit. The shrine was erected to appease him, and he was deified as Tenjin. The current main hall (honden) dates from 1591, Momoyama style - it's been under renovation since 2023 for the first time in 124 years (reopening scheduled for 2027). A temporary plant-based pavilion designed by contemporary architect Sou Fujimoto serves as replacement. The grounds hold 6,000 plum trees, including the Tobiume - the plum tree that allegedly flew from Kyoto to follow Michizane into exile.

Kushida Shrine, in Hakata's historic quarter, has been the city's protective deity since the 8th century. This is where Fukuoka's largest festival, Hakata Gion Yamakasa, begins each year. Inside, the permanent exhibition displays the 14 festival floats (yamakasa) used during the race: these wooden and bamboo structures covered with samurai and mythological hero figurines reach several meters high. The 1,000-year-old ginkgo tree in the grounds deserves an upward glance.

activities.text: Ask your accommodation where to find the nearest yatai: these small covered street stalls set up each evening on Fukuoka's sidewalks, serving tonkotsu ramen (creamy pork broth), gyoza, and yakitori skewers. Fukuoka is the only major Japanese city where yatai culture still thrives - about a hundred stalls operate nightly in the Nakasu, Tenjin, and Nagahama districts. There's no menu and you eat elbow-to-elbow - that's the essence.

If you have time, the Kyushu National Museum, just above Dazaifu Tenmangu, traces cultural exchanges between Japan and Asia from prehistory - one of Japan's four national museums. Its undulating glass-covered architecture, designed by Kikutake Kiyonori, is spectacular in itself. The permanent collection covers the maritime route between China, Korea, and the Japanese archipelago.

visits.text: 40 minutes west of Fukuoka, Sakurai Futamigaura beach in Itoshima offers one of Kyushu's most photographed views: a pristine white torii standing in the Genkai Sea, and behind it, two rocks connected by a 30-meter sacred shimenawa rope weighing about a ton. These Meoto Iwa (literally "wedded rocks") represent the deities Izanagi and Izanami from Japanese mythology - the couple who created Japan's islands. The rope is replaced annually during a high-tide ceremony in April or May. The male rock measures 11.8 meters, the female 11.2 meters. At low tide, you can walk to the torii's base. Come late afternoon: Sakurai Futamigaura is known as "the sunset Futamiura" - unlike Ise's, which is famous for sunrise.

activities.text: Sunset Road runs along Itoshima's west coast for several kilometers, lined with cafes and restaurants with sea views - a route to cycle or drive at sunset. Itoshima is also known for its artisan salt (shio) producers: some workshops offer visits and direct sales. Local cheeses (rare for Japan), Ago Bay oysters, and organic vegetables attract Fukuoka residents to the weekend market.

visits.text: Karatsu Castle, also called the "dancing crane castle" (Maizurujō), is one of the rare Japanese castles using the ocean as a natural moat - its stone walls emerge directly from the bay. Built between 1602 and 1608 by Terasawa Hirotaka using materials salvaged from the dismantled Nagoya Castle, it was then surrounded by a pine forest that, viewed from neighboring Mount Kagamiyama, resembled a crane spreading its wings. The forest has nearly disappeared on the west side, but the Nijino Matsubara pine grove - over a million black pines planted along 5 km of coast by Terasawa to protect farmland from sea winds - survives on the east, ranked among Japan's three most beautiful pine groves. The current keep dates from 1966 (concrete) but the 5th floor offers superb panoramic views over the bay, city, and pine forest.

The Hikiyama Exhibition Hall, facing Karatsu Shrine, displays year-round the 14 floats from the Karatsu Kunchi festival (November 2-4). These lacquered wooden and bamboo structures - red lions, samurai helmets, giant fish - were crafted between 1819 and 1876. If you're not there in November, it's the only way to see these artisan masterpieces up close.

activities.text: If you pass through Yobuko port, 30 minutes by bus north of Karatsu, don't miss the Asaichi morning market: 200 meters of fresh seafood stalls run by local fisherwomen, open from 7:30 am. The specialty is ikizukuri squid - squid caught that morning, prepared alive as sashimi, tentacles still moving on the plate. The experience isn't for the faint-hearted, but the taste is unparalleled.

Karatsu is one of Japan's major pottery centers (karatsu-yaki). The tradition dates back to the 16th century and today counts about 70 workshops in and around the city. Several galleries let you watch potters at work and buy directly. If ceramics interest you, plan a good hour to explore the potters' quarter.

map_keywords: Huis Ten Bosch Sasebo Dutch theme park

visits.text: Huis Ten Bosch ("House in the Forest" in Dutch) is Japan's largest theme park by area: 153 hectares, 6 km of canals, 400,000 trees planted during its construction. Opened in 1992 on a reclaimed island in Omura Bay, it recreates a 17th-century Dutch town with full-scale buildings. The name comes from Huis ten Bosch palace in The Hague, one of the Dutch royal family's residences. The location is no accident: for over two centuries, the Dutch were the only Europeans authorized to trade with Japan, via their trading post in Hirado then Dejima in Nagasaki, 35 km from here. The park has 11 attractions, 12 museums, 53 restaurants, and several hotels including one staffed by robots. Peak season is the spring tulip festival, but the nighttime illuminations (nearly 13 million LEDs) are worth the trip any season.

activities.text: Rent a bike or electric boat to explore the canals at your own pace - the best way to see the park without rushing. Canal cruises (about 30 minutes) give a different perspective on the buildings. Around 7 pm, when illuminations light up the entire artificial city, the atmosphere transforms dramatically: plan to stay for the evening.

If Huis Ten Bosch doesn't occupy your whole day, Hirado Island, 45 minutes north of Sasebo, deserves a half-day: this is where the first Dutch landed in 1609, and the Catholic church (1931) visible from the feudal castle makes a very particular photographic composition - symbol of the historical coexistence between clandestine Christianity and feudal power.

visits.text: On August 9, 1945 at 11:02 am, the "Fat Man" bomb exploded 580 meters above the Urakami district. Kokura was the primary target - but the city was covered in smoke that morning, result of bombing the previous day in Yahata. After three unsuccessful attempts over Kokura, the B-29 set course for its secondary target. Nagasaki's fate was linked to that of Kitakyushu, your departure city. Peace Park, inaugurated in 1955, sits next to the hypocenter. The Peace Statue - 10 meters of bronze, right hand pointing toward the nuclear threat, left hand extended toward peace - was created by sculptor Seibō Kitamura, a Nagasaki native. Reflect here before visiting the museum.

Mount Inasa (333 meters), west of the city, ranks among Japan's three most beautiful night views. Nagasaki city, built in a basin surrounded by hills, lights up at nightfall in a unique way - houses tier up the slopes to the water. It's nicknamed "the 10-million-dollar view." The cable car departs from the port's west bank and reaches the summit in 5 minutes. Ascend 30 minutes before sunset to watch the transition.

The Shinchi district is one of Japan's three main Chinatowns, founded in the 17th century by Chinese merchants trading through Nagasaki port. Specialties to try: champon (vegetable and seafood noodle soup, created here in the 19th century) and kakuni manju (steamed rice buns stuffed with braised pork). The artificial island of Dejima, five minutes on foot, was the only point of contact between closed Japan and the Western world between 1641 and 1853: a 15,000 m² enclosure where the Dutch were authorized to trade. It's been reconstructed and can be visited.

activities.text: Take Nagasaki's streetcar - lines in service since 1914, fixed-price tickets - to reach the Atomic Bomb Museum from Peace Park. The museum, opened in 1994 for the 50th anniversary, presents objects recovered from the site, photographs, and testimonies from hibakusha (survivors). The visit is difficult. Allow at least 1.5 hours, and know that certain rooms are particularly harrowing.

Glover Garden, on a hill overlooking the bay south of the city, was the property of Scottish merchant Thomas Blake Glover (1838-1911), one of the first industrialists to modernize Japan. Glover participated in creating the country's first railway depot and brewery. The view from its terraces over Nagasaki Bay and distant Sakurajima is splendid, especially at sunset.

visits.text: Kumamoto Castle is one of Japan's three most admired castles along with Himeji and Osaka. Its construction began in 1601 under orders from Kato Kiyomasa, and the fortress then occupied 98,000 m² with 3 large towers, 49 turrets, 18 gates, and 29 portals. The April 2016 earthquake series (magnitude 7) severely damaged the grounds - one-third of the stone walls, or 23,500 m², were compromised, and reconstruction is scheduled until 2052. The main keep reopened in June 2021 after five years of work. The damage still visible on the ramparts is part of the visit: you understand the catastrophe's power, and the stones carefully numbered and catalogued to be replaced one by one tell another story - that of Japanese patience.

Suizenji Jojuen sanctuary, 15 minutes by streetcar from the castle, is one of Kyushu's most renowned Japanese gardens. Created in 1632 by the Hosokawa clan who had just settled in Kumamoto, it reproduces in miniature the 53 stages of the Tokaido route linking Tokyo to Kyoto - including notably a 10-meter-high grass Mount Fuji. The natural water spring at the garden's depths is renowned for its purity.

activities.text: From the 14th floor of Kumamoto City Hall (free access), the plunging view over the castle grounds gives exceptional scale to the site - you grasp the fortress's immensity and its gardens. Don't miss the Sakura-no-baba Josaien complex, facing the castle: this is where Kumamon mascot (the black and red bear emblem of the prefecture) is sold in every possible variation.

Kumamoto's culinary specialty is basashi - raw horse carpaccio served with soy sauce, ginger, and garlic. If you're curious and not too squeamish, it's a taste experience found only in this region. Several izakaya in the Shimotori district serve it, along with other specialties like karashi renkon (lotus stuffed with mustard and fried).

visits.text: Beppu is Japan's hot spring capital. The city produces more hot spring water than any other onsen resort in the country. Its signature attraction is the Jigoku Meguri - the Hell Circuit. These aren't baths for bathing, but extreme-temperature springs (over 100°C) that create unique geothermal spectacles. Umi Jigoku ("sea hell") is the most impressive: a steaming cobalt-blue basin with giant water lilies capable of holding a child. Chinoike Jigoku ("blood pond hell") - blood-red due to iron oxide in the clay - is the oldest hell, documented for over 1,300 years. Tatsumaki Jigoku is a natural geyser that erupts every 30 to 40 minutes and propels 150°C water up to 30 meters.

Kamado Jigoku ("cooking pot hell") is the most diverse hell: several different-colored basins, a demon cook statue, foot and hand baths, and snacks steamed using volcanic heat. It's the best if you're only visiting one. Oniishibozu Jigoku ("monk head hell") gets its name from the gray mud bubbles that surface and resemble shaved skulls. It's also the only hell where you can actually bathe in the attached public bath, fed by the same spring.

activities.text: The hells are grouped in two zones: five in the Kannawa district to the north, two in Shibaseki 2 km away. Buy the combination pass to see all seven official ones. Count a full day to see them all - or choose the four essential ones (Umi, Kamado, Oniishibozu, Chinoike) for 4 to 5 hours. Start early morning to avoid Japanese tour groups that arrive after 10 am.

After the hells, the sand bath (sunamushi) at Kanawa Onsen is Beppu's most singular thermal experience: you're buried up to your neck in sand naturally heated to 50°C by underground springs, for about 10 to 15 minutes. Bring a towel. It's recommended for muscle pain and circulation. Different establishments offer this experience in the Kannawa district.

visits.text: Takachiho Gorge cuts 7 kilometers through a V-shaped valley carved by the Gokase River through solidified lava flows from Mount Aso, 270,000 years old. The columnar basalt cliffs reach 80 to 100 meters. The water is an emerald green that justifies the legend: according to the Kojiki (Japan's oldest collection of myths), Manai Falls - 17 meters high - was moved here by a god to supply water to a region that lacked it. Designated a national scenic spot in 1934, the gorge is accessible on foot via a 1 km trail along the cliff edge. The other option - the best - is the rental boat for 30 minutes, maximum 3 people: you find yourself at the base of the walls, within arm's reach of the waterfall. Book early morning in high season, spots go fast.

Amano Iwato Shrine, 8 km from the gorge, is Takachiho's most sacred mythological site. This is where the sun goddess Amaterasu allegedly took refuge in a cave after a dispute with her brother Susanoo, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods gathered before the cave and organized a banquet - a goddess began dancing so spectacularly that all laughed uproariously. Amaterasu, curious, partially opened her cave stone to look, and the gods prevented her from returning inside. This is the first Kagura dance - ritual art still practiced every winter night in Takachiho in 33 tableaux. Amano Yasukawara Cave, 10 minutes on foot from the shrine along the river, is covered with thousands of cairns left by visitors making wishes.

activities.text: The Kagura dance performance at Takachiho Jinja Shrine happens every evening at 8 pm for about 1 hour - a condensed version of the full night's 33 tableaux. Dancers wear traditional masks and long-sleeved costumes, accompanied by flute, drum, and cymbals. It's one of Japan's oldest forms of sacred theater. Modest entry fee, sober and genuinely inhabited performance - not to be missed if you stay overnight.

practical_info.schedule: Every evening at 8 pm at Takachiho Jinja Shrine

activities.text: Takachiho is difficult to access - since 2005, no train serves the village following a typhoon. You must arrive by bus from Kumamoto (2h) or Miyazaki (2.5h), or by car. Plan to stay overnight to have time to see the gorge, shrine, and evening performance. Village ryokan serve local specialties like mountain taro and Takachiho beef.

visits.text: Mount Aso is Japan's largest volcanic complex, with a caldera 25 km north to south and 18 km east to west - 100,000 people live inside. At the center, Nakadake (1,506 m) is the main active crater: 600 meters in diameter, 160 meters deep, and a green acid lake at the bottom. Since the 1990s, concrete bunkers have been built near the crater to shelter from projectiles in case of sudden eruption. Access depends on the day's volcanic activity - consult aso-volcano.jp before departing. The last major eruption was October 2021. If access is closed, the volcano museum broadcasts live crater images.

Kusasenrigahama grassland, between Mounts Kishima and Eboshi, is a one-kilometer-diameter basin where horses and cows graze freely facing Nakadake's smoke - one of Kyushu's most photographed landscapes. In autumn, pampas grass (susuki) turns golden. Daikanbo Observatory, on the caldera's northern periphery, offers the most spectacular panoramic view of Aso's five peaks - their recumbent profile evokes a reclining Buddha. It's also one of the best spots for the sea of clouds in autumn and winter, when morning mist fills the caldera.

activities.text: Komezuka, a perfectly symmetrical 50-meter volcanic cone covered in green grass, is one of Aso's iconic symbols. Locals say it resembles an upside-down bowl of rice - "kome" means rice. It photographs ideally from the road crossing the caldera, stop at the designated parking area.

For those denied crater access, helicopter flights from the launch zone south of the caldera offer a plunging view over Nakadake and its fumaroles otherwise unobtainable. Count about 7 minutes of flight. Hot springs in the Aso region - notably those at Kurokawa Onsen, 1 hour north - are among Kyushu's most renowned for their traditional ryokan with outdoor baths.

visits.text: Sengan-en Garden, created in 1658 by the 19th lord of the Shimazu clan, is the masterpiece of shakkei - the art of "borrowed scenery": the garden is designed to integrate Sakurajima volcano and Kinko Bay as natural backdrop, creating the illusion that the composition extends infinitely. Across 50,000 m², this park of the Shimazu family villa houses historic rooms open to the public (Edward VIII and Nicholas II were received here), a shrine, and the Shoko Shuseikan museum - installed in Japan's first modern factory, built by the Shimazu in the 1850s with techniques learned from a Dutch manual. In 2015, the site was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the category "Sites of Japan's Meiji Industrial Revolution."

35 km southwest of Kagoshima, Chiran is a dual town. On one side, an Edo-period samurai quarter with seven classified dry gardens, nestled behind high stone walls. On the other, the Peace Museum dedicated to kamikaze pilots, built in 1975 on the site of the former airbase. Of the 1,036 Special Attack Corps pilots who died during the Battle of Okinawa, 439 departed from Chiran. The museum preserves their farewell letters, personal effects, photographs, and four original aircraft including a Mitsubishi Zero recovered from the sea in 1980. The visit is silent and heavy. Allow 1.5 hours.

activities.text: Take the 15-minute ferry from Kagoshima port to reach Sakurajima - one of the world's most active volcanoes, with minor eruptions several times a week for decades. Yunohira Observatory, at 373 meters altitude on the volcano's flanks, offers the closest authorized view of Minamidake crater. The Arimura Cape trail lets you walk on solidified lava flows. Keep car windows closed - fine ash infiltrates everywhere.

Shiroyama Observatory, on the city's heights, offers the classic panoramic view over Kagoshima and Sakurajima at sunset. The hill is also the site of Saigo Takamori's last stand - the "last samurai" - during the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion. A plaque marks the exact spot where he died. The walk through Shiroyama forest (30 minutes) is pleasant and accessible.

visits.text: Yakushima is a 505 km² island designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993 - one of Japan's first natural sites to receive the honor. Seventy-five percent of its area is covered in forest, and a local proverb says "it rains 35 days a month" - not far from truth, with over 8,000 mm of annual precipitation in the highlands. This humidity has created a unique ecosystem: 1,900 plant species, moss on everything stationary for more than 10 minutes, and thousand-year-old Japanese cedars (yakusugi) rooted since the Jomon era. Shiratani Unsuikyo forest, accessible from Miyanoura port, is the one Hayao Miyazaki traversed in the 1990s before creating the world of Princess Mononoke - when you walk among the twisted roots and moss thick as cushions, you recognize the film.

The Jomon Sugi, Yakushima's most famous cedar, is estimated between 2,300 and 7,000 years old depending on calculation methods. It measures 25 meters high and 16 meters in circumference. To reach it requires 8 to 10 hours round trip over 22 km from the Arakawa trailhead - a long hike but without technical difficulty, on old forest rails from the era when cryptomeria wood was cut to roof temples throughout Japan. The observation platform 10 meters from the tree dates from 1996, installed to reduce soil compaction by tourists. Plan a 5 am departure from the port (Arakawa shuttle bus) to return before 5 pm.

activities.text: From Kagoshima, the jetfoil (hydrofoil) reaches Miyanoura in 1h40 or Anbo in 2h. In high season, book ahead. There are also 35-minute flights from Kagoshima airport. Once on the island, local buses serve the main trailheads, but having a car gives much more freedom. Bring complete waterproof gear: rain can arrive anytime, even in fine weather in town.

For non-hikers, the Yakusugi Land trail (starting at 1,000 m altitude) offers 30 to 150-minute loops through thousand-year-old cryptomerias on wooden boardwalks - accessible to all. Oko-no-taki waterfall (88 meters high) is Yakushima's tallest, visible from the road. Nagata beach (west coast) is the North Pacific's most important loggerhead turtle nesting site - females arrive May to July, at night.

seo.h1_title: Kyushu & Yakushima Circuit: Volcanoes and Ancient Forests
seo.intro_paragraph: From Kitakyushu to Yakushima, this circuit traverses thirteen days across an island that's anything but tranquil. Samurai castles and medieval quarters in the north, boiling springs of Beppu's hells and smoking crater of Mount Aso in the center, Nagasaki's memory and Yakushima's thousand-year-old primeval forest in the south - Kyushu packs a density of history and nature few Japanese itineraries can match.
seo.seo_hook: Beppu's hells, Aso crater, Takachiho gorge, Yakushima cedars: Kyushu packs 13 days of extraordinary Japan into one island.
featured_list: Beppu: seven geothermal hells including a cobalt-blue 100°C basin and a 30-meter geyser
Aso: Japan's largest active volcano with a 120 km circumference caldera
Takachiho: V-shaped gorge sculpted by Mount Aso, mythological birthplace of Amaterasu
Yakushima: thousand-year-old cedars in a UNESCO primeval forest that inspired Princess Mononoke

itineraries.title: Tokai and Japanese Alps Circuit: Waterfalls and Villages
itineraries.subtitle: 14 days among sacred waterfalls of Mount Fuji, suspension bridges over emerald lakes, UNESCO thatched villages and thousand-year-old shrines
itineraries.notes: SEASONALITY WARNING: this itinerary combines sites whose optimal periods do NOT overlap (Inabe plum blossoms = March, Toyone shibazakura = May-June, Hirizo Beach = July-September, Korankei foliage = November, Tsushima wisteria = late April-early May). It's designed as a regional catalogue - travelers will need to adapt the sequence or skip certain stops depending on their travel dates. Monet Pond (Day 9) is at its best from June to September. Consider purchasing a Japan Rail Pass for Shinkansen connections. Return from Shima is possible via Kintetsu's Kashikojima Station (Nagoya in ~2h30).
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-May and October-November, temperatures 15-23°C, ideal for the Alps and coast. Avoid the rainy season (mid-June to mid-July) and summer (oppressive humid heat, possible typhoons). Winter in Shirakawa-go: heavy snow, bring appropriate gear.

map_keywords: Mt Fuji World Heritage Center Fujinomiya

visits.text: Shiraito Falls awaits you at the foot of Mount Fuji's southwest slope: a curved 20-meter-high, 150-meter-wide cliff where springwater filtered through the volcano bursts forth in hundreds of white threads—hence the name "Shiraito" (silk thread). It's not a river feeding the falls: the Fuji's groundwater takes between 10 and 300 years to emerge here, at a rate of 1.5 tons per second, at 12°C year-round. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage component in 2013 as part of Mount Fuji's cultural site, these falls served as an ascetic training ground for pilgrim monks during the Edo period. Descend the steps to the basin—the mist is refreshing even in midsummer.

Just a 5-minute walk upstream, don't miss Otodome Falls, narrower but more powerful, with a 25-meter vertical drop. Their name means "to stop the sound": according to legend, the Soga brothers wanted to silence the waterfall's roar so they could plot their revenge in complete secrecy. The contrast with Shiraito's gentleness is striking.

Head back down to Fujinomiya to visit Fujisan Hongu Sengen Taisha, the head shrine of Japan's 1,300 Sengen shrines. Its origins date back to 27 BC, when it was erected to calm Mount Fuji's eruptions. The current buildings were constructed by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1604, and the main hall (honden) displays a unique two-story architectural style called "sengen-zukuri," designated an Important Cultural Property. In spring, 500 cherry trees bloom along the Sakura no Baba approach—it's one of the region's premier hanami spots.

Right next to the shrine, stop by the sacred Wakutama Pond, a Special National Natural Monument. Mount Fuji's snowmelt water surges through the volcanic rock with almost surreal clarity—pilgrims purified themselves here before beginning their ascent of the mountain. The Mount Fuji World Heritage Centre, just steps away, offers an interactive exhibition about the volcano with an observation terrace facing Fuji if the sky is clear.

activities.text: Try Fujinomiya yakisoba, a local specialty of stir-fried noodles made with particularly elastic noodles, lard and sardine flakes, all cooked with Mount Fuji's spring water. Stalls serve them near the falls and in the town centre.

visits.text: Hirizo Beach is nicknamed "the last unexplored area of Izu"—and with good reason: it's only accessible by boat from Nakagi Port (10-minute crossing). The water here boasts Okinawa-rivalling transparency, with visibility exceeding 7 meters thanks to the Kuroshio Current sweeping away sediment. You'll see corals, clownfish, schools of sardines and occasionally sea turtles. Be warned: the beach is only open from early July through late September, it's rocky (bring water shoes), and August weekends are packed—come on weekdays or in September for relative calm.

If you have time late in the day, push on to Cape Irozaki, the southern tip of the Izu Peninsula. Its white lighthouse offers a sweeping Pacific panorama, and on clear days you'll spot the offshore Izu Islands. It's also a prime sunset viewing point.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Hirizo Beach—outfitters at Nakagi Port rent masks, snorkels and wetsuits. A guide who knows the day's best spots will take you to the most fish-rich zones. Plan a full day.

visits.text: The Dream Suspension Bridge (Yume no Tsuribashi) was voted one of the world's 10 suspension bridges to cross before you die by TripAdvisor. Ninety meters long and perched 8 meters above a dam lake of almost unreal cobalt blue (the Tyndall effect renders the water turquoise on sunny days), this wooden bridge sways noticeably underfoot—maximum 10 people at a time. Tradition holds that you should make a love wish at its centre. Be prepared: after crossing, you must climb 304 steep steps. Allow 30 minutes' walk from the hot spring village of Sumatakyo Onsen, through a tunnel renowned for its "healing wind."

Okuoikojo Station, on the Oigawa Railway's Ikawa Line, appears to float in the middle of Nagashima Dam's emerald lake. Two red bridges of 195 and 286 meters connect it to the shores—you can walk across the pedestrian footbridge (the Rainbow Bridge) for a complete panorama of the station, lake and Southern Alps mountains. On weekends, a small pop-up café opens in the station chalet.

activities.text: Take the Oigawa Railway steam train from Senzu Station—four locomotives built in the 1940s are still in service. The journey crosses terraced tea valleys and forested gorges. In summer, a Thomas the Tank Engine train runs for families.

Relax in the onsen baths of Sumatakyo Onsen late in the day. The sulphurous water is renowned for softening skin—the Japanese call these springs "bijin no yu" (beauty bath). Several ryokan offer day-use bath access.

visits.text: Mount Chausu (1,358 m), Aichi Prefecture's highest peak, hosts the "Heavenly Flower Corridor": 400,000 moss phlox plants in six varieties—hot pink, white, light blue, purple—carpeting the summit slope from mid-May through early June. The spectacle is all the more striking as the Southern Alps rise in the background. Ride the panoramic chairlift to the summit and search for the heart-shaped pattern hidden in the flowerbed—the Japanese say it brings good fortune in love.

At the summit, Chausu Terrace offers an unobstructed view of the Southern Alps range—it's one of the few easily accessible viewpoints at this altitude in the region. On clear days, the panorama extends for dozens of kilometres.

activities.text: Toyone village is known for its mountain-water sturgeon farming—try the "Royal Fish," a local speciality served as dumplings or sashimi in village restaurants. Surprising in the Japanese mountains.
In summer (July-August), the Chausu plateau offers outdoor activities: trout fishing, canoeing, hiking. At night, far from any light pollution, the starry sky is spectacular—you might even spot deer.

visits.text: Korankei is THE autumn foliage spot for the entire Tokai region—about 4,000 Japanese maples planted 400 years ago by San'ei, the 11th monk of Kojakuji Temple, blanket Mount Iimori in crimson and gold each November. The vermillion Taigetsukyo Bridge spanning the Tomoe River is the most famous photo spot. In the evening during the Maple Festival (throughout November), the mountain is illuminated until 9 pm—the golden effect on the leaves is striking. Off-season, come in March for wild violets or in spring for tender green shoots.

Push on to Asuke town, 10 minutes from Korankei—its late Edo period houses (1776-1830) make it Aichi's first Traditional Building Preservation District. The Sanshu Asuke Yashiki museum-village offers weaving and indigo dyeing workshops in a mountain setting. Try gohei mochi (grilled rice skewers with sweet-savoury miso sauce)—it's THE local speciality.

If you have energy, climb to Asuke Castle, reconstructed based on archaeological excavations—a rarity in Japan. From the keep at 301 meters altitude, the view over the town and forested valley is the area's finest. Allow 40 minutes' walk from Korankei.

activities.text: Try gohei mochi at the stalls in Korankei or Asuke—these grilled rice skewers glazed with sweet-savoury miso-walnut sauce are the region's mountain speciality. Pair them with an ayu (freshwater trout) grilled on a stick.

visits.text: Cape Irago Lighthouse, at the tip of the Atsumi Peninsula, ranks among Japan's 50 finest lighthouses. Built in 1929, it dominates the point where the Pacific Ocean, Ise Bay and Mikawa Bay converge—the 360° panorama is breathtaking. On clear days, you'll glimpse the Shima Peninsula opposite. Come late in the day: the sunset bathes everything in orange.

A few minutes from the lighthouse, Koiji Beach ("love road") is a pilgrimage site for Japanese couples. Right next door, the Hinode Stone Gate is a natural rock arch through which the sun rises in October and February—a spectacle photographers await each year.

activities.text: The Atsumi Peninsula is known for its melon and chrysanthemum cultivation. Depending on the season, you'll find farms offering fruit picking (melons in summer, strawberries in spring). Enquire at the local tourist office.

visits.text: The Tsushima Tenno Wisteria Festival is one of Japan's most spectacular: a giant 275-meter-long trellis covering 5,034 square meters, with 12 wisteria varieties forming a purple, white and pink curtain from late April through early May. Walk beneath—the flower clusters brush your hair and the fragrance is intoxicating. In the evening, illuminations transform the trellis into a luminous vault. Outside the season, the park remains pleasant but the appeal is really limited to the wisteria.

Tsushima Shrine, neighbouring the wisteria park, is dedicated to the kami of the sea and protection against epidemics. Its summer festival (July) is inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list—lantern-lit boats descend the river.

activities.text: Tsushima is close to Nagoya—if you have free time, stroll along the canals crisscrossing this former merchant town. Local shops serve kushikatsu (fried breaded skewers) and tenmusu (onigiri with tempura shrimp), Owari region specialities.

visits.text: Yoro Falls (養老の滝), ranked among Japan's 100 most beautiful waterfalls, tumbles 30 meters into a rocky basin in the heart of dense forest. Legend has it that a dutiful son discovered a spring whose water turned into sake—Emperor Genshō was so impressed that he renamed the imperial era "Yoro" in 717. The trail from the car park climbs 30 minutes through the forest—in autumn, red maples frame the falls. Arrive early in the morning to avoid weekend crowds.

On your way back down, detour to the Site of Reversible Destiny (養老天命反転地), a contemporary art park designed by Arakawa and Madeline Gins. The deliberately destabilising terrain (slopes, uneven ground, colour maze) is meant to "reverse" your destiny. It's disorienting, fun, and completely unique in Japan. Wear flat shoes.

activities.text: Yoro Park is pleasant for a stroll—between cherry blossoms in spring and maples in autumn, there's always something in bloom. Stalls sell mochi and local green tea.

visits.text: "Monet's Pond" (モネの池) is actually just an irrigation pond for Nemichi Shrine, but its transparency and water lilies have made it an Instagram sensation. The spring water is so clear that the orange, white and golden koi seem to swim in mid-air above the sandy bottom—the effect recalls Monet's Water Lilies. The best period runs from June to September when the water lilies bloom. Come in the morning: the flowers are open and the low-angle light penetrates the water. The pond is small—allow 15-20 minutes on site.

Seki has been Japan's cutlery capital for 700 years—blacksmiths here forged katanas for samurai. Visit the traditional forging museum to see hand-forging demonstrations and understand ancestral techniques. You can also buy professional-quality kitchen knives in the district's shops.

activities.text: Twice a year (early October and early April), Seki hosts a forging festival with public blade-making demonstrations—flames, sparks and hammering. If your dates align, it's a rare spectacle.

visits.text: Shirakawa-go (UNESCO-listed since 1995) is a mountain village where 114 gassho-zukuri farmhouses survive—literally "hands joined in prayer," referring to the extreme roof pitch designed to bear snowfalls sometimes exceeding 2 meters. Some houses are over 250 years old and built without a single nail, using a wood-joinery system. Start with Wada House, the largest and oldest (over 300 years), designated an Important Cultural Property—climb to the 4th floor to see the space where silkworms were raised.

Climb to Shiroyama Observatory (15 minutes' walk from the village) for Shirakawa-go's most famous panorama: thatched roofs aligned in the valley, framed by mountains and rice fields. It's THE postcard shot—in winter with snow, it's even more spectacular. The winter illumination (6 evenings in January-February, mandatory reservation) draws thousands of visitors.

Myozenji Temple and its two gassho-zukuri annexes form the village's finest ensemble—the temple bell is broadcast by NHK at New Year. The small attached museum traces the history of rural mountain life.

activities.text: Spend a night in a gassho-zukuri minshuku (family guesthouse)—you'll sleep on futon and tatami, and the kaiseki dinner is prepared with local products: Hida beef, artisanal tofu, river fish. In the early morning, when day-trippers haven't yet arrived, the village is absolutely peaceful.
Try doburoku, a cloudy, unfiltered sake produced locally. Shirakawa Hachiman Shrine hosts a doburoku festival in October—the brew is offered to visitors.

visits.text: Inabe Plum Grove (いなべ市農業公園 梅林公園) is the Tokai region's largest: 38 hectares, 100 varieties, over 4,000 trees. From early to late March, plum blossoms open in a gradient of red, pink and white—climb to the observatory at the hilltop to embrace the panorama with the Suzuka Mountains as backdrop. The delicate fragrance of ume (plums) perfumes the entire domain. The Ume Matsuri (plum festival) is held in March with plum-product tastings and picking.

The Suzuka Mountains rising behind the grove offer accessible hiking trails—Mount Ryozen (1,099 m) is one of the range's most popular. If you don't have time to hike, at least stop at the Inabe River gorges, where turquoise water contrasts with limestone rocks. It's on the route between Shirakawa-go and Inabe.

activities.text: Take advantage of the festival to try local specialities made from umeboshi (pickled plum) and umeshu (plum liqueur). Some farms offer plum picking that you can take home.

visits.text: The 48 Waterfalls of Akame (赤目四十八滝) cascade along 4 km of forested gorge—in reality, there are well over 48, but the "Five Waterfalls of Akame" are the trail's stars. Ninai Falls, which splits into two parallel streams before rejoining, is the gorge's symbol. The trail is ranked among Japan's 100 best forest bathing sites and 100 finest waters. Allow 1.5 hours one-way to the trail's end—the path is well-maintained but with stairs and wet passages. Bring hiking shoes.

activities.text: Akame Gorge was a training ground for Iga clan ninja—at the trail entrance, a small interactive museum offers ninja technique demonstrations and shuriken throwing. Fun for families.
After the hike, relax in one of Nabari's onsen—the town has several hot springs along the riverside. Ask your accommodation about baths open to day visitors.

visits.text: The Meoto Iwa (Married Rocks) of Futami are two sacred rocks linked by a braided rice-straw shimenawa rope—the larger measures 9 m, the smaller 4 m. From May to July, the sun rises between the two rocks, and in exceptional weather you'll glimpse Mount Fuji on the horizon. The rope is changed three times a year (May, September, December) during a Shinto ceremony. Come at sunrise—it's the most powerful moment, and there's almost no one around.

Ise Jingu is Japan's most sacred shrine—dedicated to Amaterasu, sun goddess and ancestor of the imperial family. The Naiku (Inner Shrine) is rebuilt identically to itself every 20 years since the 7th century (the next reconstruction is scheduled for 2033). You won't see the main building, hidden behind palisades, but the path through the centuries-old cedar forest and the Uji Bridge spanning the Isuzu River are themselves a pilgrimage. Allow 1 to 2 hours.

Leaving the Naiku, dive into Okage Yokocho, a recreated Edo-style shopping street running alongside the shrine. It's the place to try Ise udon (thick, soft noodles in dark broth), akafuku mochi (rice dumplings coated in red bean paste, a specialty since 1707) and tekone-zushi (marinated bonito sashimi on vinegared rice).

activities.text: If time permits, visit the Geku (Outer Shrine), dedicated to the kami of food, located 6 km from the Naiku. Less crowded, it offers an even more contemplative atmosphere. Traditional pilgrimage begins with the Geku before the Naiku.

visits.text: Goza Shirahama Beach is ranked among Japan's 100 best swimming beaches—its white sand and cobalt-blue water evoke the tropics rather than central Japan. The waves are gentle and the depth increases very gradually, making it a good spot for families. It's also popular with surfers when the swell picks up. Open in summer, the beach has showers and changing rooms.

Climb to Yokoyama Observatory for a bird's-eye view of Ago Bay and its dozens of pine-covered islets—this is where cultured pearls have been cultivated since Mikimoto succeeded in producing the first cultured pearl in 1893. The ria (indented coastline) landscape is one of the Shima Peninsula's most photographed.

activities.text: In Osatsu, you can meet the ama—traditional female divers who have free-dived for abalone, sea urchins and seaweed for centuries. Some fisherwomen's huts (amagoya) welcome visitors for a fireside grilled seafood meal, served by the ama themselves. Book in advance.

seo.h1_title: Tokai and Japanese Alps Circuit: Waterfalls and Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: From Mount Fuji's sacred waterfalls to Shirakawa-go's thatched roofs, this 14-day circuit traverses central Japan far from the Tokyo and Kyoto crowds. Plunge into Hirizo's turquoise waters, cross a suspension bridge over an emerald lake at Sumatakyo, witness Korankei's blazing autumn foliage, and finish with the Ise Jingu pilgrimage and Shima's ama divers.
seo.seo_hook: Mount Fuji waterfalls, snow-covered gassho-zukuri villages, emerald lake suspension bridge, Monet's pond: intimate Japan far from crowds.

itineraries.title: San'In and Hiroshima Road Trip: Japan's Secret Coast
itineraries.subtitle: From Tottori's dunes to Nagato's torii gates, along the Sea of Japan and its ancient shrines.
itineraries.notes: The Hamada-Okayama stretch is long (approximately 170 km) and can be split into two stages if traveling at a slower pace. Motonosumi Shrine is not accessible by public transport—a car is required for the final portion of the route. In winter (December-March), Bitchu Matsuyama Castle may be closed or difficult to access due to snow.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May and October-November, temperatures 15-24°C, ideal for the San'In coast. Avoid January-February (heavy snow on the Sea of Japan side) and July-August (humid heat +30°C, tsuyu rainy season). Winter is harsh in this region.

visits.text: The Tottori Sand Dunes stretch 16 km from east to west and 2.4 km from north to south—they're the largest coastal dunes accessible to visitors in Japan, and the only ones designated a National Natural Monument. They were born over 100,000 years ago: sand from the Chugoku Mountains, carried by the Sendai River to the Sea of Japan, was pushed back to shore by currents and winds that sculpted this ever-shifting landscape. Climb up to Umanose—the 'horse's back'—a ridge that peaks at 47 meters and from which the sea and dunes extend in every direction. Bring a hat and water: in summer, the sand reaches 50°C.

The Sand Museum, right on the edge of the dunes, is the world's only museum entirely devoted to sand sculptures—and it's been housed in a permanent building since 2012. Each year, world-renowned sculptors create monumental works on a different theme (in 2026, Spain). What makes the place fascinating is that everything will be destroyed in January to start over from scratch. Plan on 45 minutes to an hour to tour the exhibits.

activities.text: Sandboarding and paragliding are the two flagship activities at the dunes—operators offer sessions on-site, including for beginners. Since the sand is soft, falls are harmless. If you prefer contemplation over action, take the chairlift to the Sakyu Center observation platform: the view of the coast and waves of sand is striking, especially in late afternoon when the raking light draws shadows along the ridges.

In winter (from mid-December to March), snow covers the dunes and transforms them into a landscape of snow-covered ridges that's absolutely unique. There are very few visitors, and the undulations of sand beneath the snow create patterns you won't see anywhere else. If you're there during this period, don't miss the nighttime illuminations in mid-December.

visits.text: The Utsubuki-Tamagawa district of Kurayoshi is one of Japan's Important Preservation Districts for Groups of Traditional Buildings—about a hundred merchant houses and warehouses built between the Edo period and the Taisho era line the small Tamagawa River. The visual signature of the place: white walls on top, cedar planks blackened by the sun below, and red-brick sekishu tiles imported from Iwami for their resistance to frost. The main street Honmachi-dori and the warehouses along the river form two distinct atmospheres—plan at least an hour to get lost in both. Red and black carp glide under the small stone bridges.

The Makita Residence—also known as Kurayoshi Yodoya—is the country house of one of Osaka's greatest merchants from the Edo period, the House of Yodoya. The fact that such a figure maintained a foothold in Kurayoshi says much about the town's commercial importance at the time. It's open to visitors free of charge.

activities.text: The 15 red tile pavilions (Akagawara, numbered 1 to 15) now house local product shops, cafés, and artisan workshops—notably sake and soy sauce producers whose buildings haven't changed since the Meiji era. This is also where you'll find Kurayoshi Gasuri, a traditional patterned textile that artisans still weave by hand. A good reason to push open a few doors.

If you pass through in spring, Utsubuki Park at the foot of Mount Utsubuki (204 m) is one of Japan's hundred most beautiful hanami sites, with more than 4,000 cherry trees and 40,000 azaleas. The rest of the year, the path that climbs to the summit offers a lovely view of the town and its red roofs.

visits.text: The Adachi Museum of Art, opened in 1970 by Yasugi-native entrepreneur Zenko Adachi, houses the world's largest collection of works by Yokoyama Taikan—120 pieces on permanent display—as well as works by Takeuchi Seiho, Kawai Gyokudo, and Uemura Shoen. But what makes this museum truly exceptional is that the founder considered his garden a living painting: 165,000 m² of gardens in six different styles (karesansui, pines and white gravel, moss, pond…) form a composition that you contemplate from the museum windows as you would look at a framed painting. Don't miss the Kikaku waterfall, built in 1978 to evoke Taikan's painting 'Nachi Falls.'

activities.text: The Adachi Museum garden has been ranked number 1 among Japanese gardens without interruption since 2003 by the American magazine Sukiya Living, which specializes in Japanese gardens—beating out Kyoto's famous Katsura Imperial Villa garden every single year. It also holds three stars in the Michelin Green Guide. What makes this ranking particularly striking: the Adachi gardens are not accessible on foot—they can only be viewed from inside the museum, like ever-changing paintings according to the hour and season. In autumn, the red maples transform the karesansui into something unreal.

The free shuttle from Yasugi Station (every 30 minutes, 20-minute ride) eliminates parking concerns. If you have time after the museum, the town of Yasugi is also the region's ceramics center—a few workshops offer demonstrations.

map_keywords: Mizuki Shigeru Road Sakaiminato yokai statues

visits.text: Mizuki Shigeru Road runs from Sakaiminato Station and extends 800 meters to the memorial museum—along this route, 177 bronze yokai statues welcome passersby from pedestals of all sizes. The road was inaugurated in 1993 with only 23 statues; the first year, 20,000 visitors came; the following year, 280,000. Mizuki Shigeru (1922-2015), a Sakaiminato native, lost his left arm during World War II and didn't achieve success as a manga artist until age 43 with GeGeGe no Kitaro (1965), adapted into anime six times. In the evening, the statues are illuminated and yokai silhouettes are projected onto the ground—the atmosphere changes dramatically.

The Mizuki Shigeru Memorial Museum, opened in 2003, presents approximately 700 original works by the manga artist, rotated every six months. Permanent exhibitions mix original drawings, resin character statues, and video screens to immerse visitors in the world of yokai. Audio guides are available in five languages.

activities.text: The yokai stamp rally is the town's game: pick up a booklet at the station tourist information center, and collect stamps at shops and sites all along Mizuki Shigeru Road. At the end, bring back the completed booklet to receive a gift. On-site, restaurants offer dishes with evocative names (Kitaro onigiri, Medama-Oyaji seafood bowl)—Sakaiminato is first and foremost a fishing port: the fresh fish here is remarkable.

visits.text: Matsue Castle is one of the twelve original keeps still standing in Japan—and one of five designated National Treasures (along with Himeji, Matsumoto, Hikone, and Inuyama). Built between 1607 and 1611 by Lord Horio Yoshiharu, founder of Matsue, it's nicknamed Chidori-jo ('Plover Castle') for the shape of its eaves that recall the bird's outstretched wings. Its dark color comes from a dye made from unripe persimmons macerated for five years. From the Tengu-no-Ma at the top—a room open to the four winds—the 360° view over Lake Shinji and the city is the best in the region. The stairs are steep and the steps uneven: wear closed-toe shoes.

Hinomisaki Lighthouse, a 20-minute drive west of Izumo Taisha, is Japan's tallest stone lighthouse: 43.65 meters high, or 63 meters above sea level. Built in 1903, it's still in service and appears on the IALA's list of the world's 100 historic lighthouses. From the 163 spiral steps, on clear days you'll glimpse the Oki Islands on the northern horizon—once a place of exile for political prisoners.

activities.text: The Horikawa moat boat cruise around the castle lasts about 50 minutes and passes under bridges so low that the boat's roof automatically lowers. In winter, kotatsu (heated tables) built into the boats transform the cruise into a particularly pleasant experience. Combined castle + boat tickets are available—ask at the castle entrance.

Shiomi Nawate Street runs along the north side of the castle and preserves several samurai residences from the Edo period. This is also where you'll find the house of Lafcadio Hearn (Koizumi Yakumo), the Irish-Greek writer who settled in Matsue in 1890 and became one of the first Western authors to document Japanese culture and ghosts. The sunset over Lake Shinji from the banks is selected among Japan's 100 most beautiful sunsets.

visits.text: Izumo Taisha is one of Japan's two great Shinto shrines along with Ise Jingu—and the only one whose exact founding date is unknown, so ancient is it. The Kojiki, Japan's oldest chronicle (712), already mentions the site. The principal deity, Okuninushi no Okami, is the god of marriage and destinies—which is why you clap four times here instead of two: twice for yourself, twice for the person you love or are seeking. The current prayer hall (Haiden) was rebuilt in 1981; the great main hall (Honden, 24 m high) dates from 1744 in the Taisha-zukuri style, the oldest Shinto architectural style in Japan. Take time to walk along the two rows of pines on the approach path: the central corridor is reserved for the gods.

The giant shimenawa hanging in the Kaguraden (the sacred dance hall) is Japan's largest ritual rope: 13.5 meters long, 5.2 tons. It's handmade by artisans from Shimane Prefecture, and replaced approximately every six years. Its twist is reversed compared to all other shrines in Japan—a sign of Izumo's very ancient independence from the dominant Shinto system. The small rabbit statues scattered throughout the grounds recall the legend of the white rabbit of Inaba that Okuninushi saved, an act that earned him the love of Princess Yakamihime.

activities.text: Every year in October (the 10th lunar month), all the gods of Japan are said to gather at Izumo for their annual assembly—which is why this month is called Kannazuki ('month without gods') everywhere in the country, except at Izumo where they say Kamiarizuki ('month with gods'). If you're there during this period, the atmosphere is particularly striking. Outside of October, the approach to the shrine—a 700-meter-long street—is lined with Izumo soba shops, the local noodles served stacked in three superimposed bowls: a specialty not to be missed.

The Shimane Museum of Ancient Izumo, right next to the shrine, presents reconstructions of what the Honden was like in medieval times—it would have reached 48 meters high, making it the tallest wooden structure in Japan at the time. In 2000, excavations uncovered immense pillars formed from trios of logs bound by iron hoops, confirming the plausibility of these extraordinary dimensions. Note: the museum is closed for renovation until September 2026.

map_keywords: Hamada coast Sea of Japan Shimane

visits.text: The Shimane Aquas Aquarium in Hamada is the only aquarium in western Japan to host belugas—these white cetaceans nicknamed 'sea canaries' for their varied vocalizations. The bubble ring shows, where belugas create and play with air rings, are the most renowned. The aquarium also presents some 400 marine species. Plan 1.5 to 2 hours on-site.

activities.text: Hamada is a transit stop between Izumo and Okayama, but if you have time, make a detour of about 30 minutes to Iwami Ginzan: the old silver mine, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2007, supplied Japan with much of its silver in the 16th and 17th centuries. Mine tunnels are accessible to visit in the forest. The Iwami coastal region also merits a stop for a fresh fish meal.

map_keywords: Seto Ohashi Bridge Okayama Kojima view

visits.text: Korakuen Garden, on the banks of the Asahi River facing Okayama Castle, is one of the three great Edo-period gardens in Japan, along with Kenrokuen in Kanazawa and Kairakuen in Mito. It was created between 1687 and 1700 by Ikeda Tsunamasa, lord of Okayama. What distinguishes it: its large open lawns crossed by canals, its rice paddies still cultivated in June, its tea fields, and its aviaries where red-crowned cranes take flight on special occasions. From almost anywhere in the garden, the black castle is silhouetted in the background.

Kibitsu Shrine is one of the most architecturally interesting shrines in Japan: its style called Kibitsu-zukuri is unique in the world, with a double roof in adjoining gables. A covered corridor of 360 meters follows the wooded hills behind the main shrine—walking it alone in the morning is an experience apart. The legend associated with the place—Kibitsuhiko fighting the demon Ura—is the origin of the tale of Momotaro, the Peach Boy, Okayama's most beloved hero.

activities.text: The Great Seto Bridge (Seto Ohashi) connects Honshu to Shikoku over 9.4 km of two-level viaducts—trains below, cars above—across six successive bridges. From the Washuzan viewing area at Cape Kojima, you see it stretch until it disappears in the distance over the Seto Inland Sea. Allow 30 minutes for this detour if you have a car.

Okayama Castle, nicknamed Ujo ('Crow Castle') for its black-lacquered exterior walls, is a 1966 reconstruction—the original was bombed in 1945. The interior is a museum dedicated to the history of the castle and its Ikeda lords. From the top floor, the view of Korakuen and the river is the best in the city.

map_keywords: Kurashiki Bikan Historical Quarter white storehouses

visits.text: The Bikan Historical Quarter of Kurashiki developed in the 17th century as a rice distribution center on the Seto Inland Sea. The white-walled, black-tiled warehouses that line the Kurashiki River—bordered by weeping willows and crossed by small stone bridges—have remained virtually unchanged since the Edo period. The river can now be traveled by boat steered by boatmen in kimono and straw hats. Arrive early in the morning or in the evening to avoid tour group crowds.

The Ohara Museum of Art is Japan's first private museum devoted to Western art, opened in 1930 by textile magnate Ohara Magosaburo to commemorate his painter friend Kojima Torajiro, who died the previous year. Ohara had financed Kojima's travels to Europe to purchase works—it's this collection that forms the museum's core. You'll find Monet, El Greco, Renoir, Gauguin, Cézanne, Picasso, and in the garden sculptures by Rodin and Isamu Noguchi. The building itself, neoclassical Greek temple-style, is designated an Important Cultural Property.

Kurashiki Ivy Square is a former Meiji-era spinning mill, built in 1888 and converted into a hotel, dining, and craft workshop complex. The red brick facade covered in climbing ivy is one of the city's most popular photo spots.

activities.text: The old warehouses of the Bikan Quarter house shops selling jeans (Kurashiki has been Japan's denim capital since the 1960s, and Kojima—15 km away—is the first place where jeans were manufactured in Japan), Bizen ceramics, artisan paper, and sweet specialties. If you enjoy browsing shops, plan easily an extra half-day for this quarter alone.

map_keywords: Bitchu Matsuyama Castle Takahashi mountain castle
Unkai Observatory sea of clouds Takahashi

visits.text: Bitchu Matsuyama Castle is the only mountain castle among the twelve original keeps still standing in Japan, and the highest: it perches atop Mount Gagyu at 430 meters altitude. A fortress has existed on this site since 1240; the current two-story keep dates from 1683 and is designated an Important Cultural Property. From the Fuigo parking area, allow 20 minutes of mountain trail walking to reach the main gate—wear closed-toe shoes. At the summit, the view over the city of Takahashi and the valley below is breathtaking.

Raikyu-ji Temple, down in the city, has a karesansui dry garden attributed to Kobori Enshu—the famous tea master and garden architect of the early 17th century who was at one time governor of the castle. The garden is a model example of the Edo period genre. Allow 30 to 45 minutes on-site.

activities.text: From mid-October to March, when weather conditions align—cold nights, dewy mornings—a sea of clouds (unkai) forms in the valley and surrounds the castle, which then appears to float in the sky. The phenomenon is visible from the Unkai Observatory, accessible only by car or shared taxi from the station (advance reservation required). The ideal viewing window is between 6am and 8am.

practical_info.booking: Shared taxi to be reserved the day before at the station tourist office

activities.text: The city of Takahashi—nicknamed the 'Little Kyoto of Bitchu'—preserves two original samurai residences in the Ishibiyacho district, 15 minutes on foot from the station. This is one of the rare places in Japan where you can see such dwellings still partly inhabited by their descendant owners.

visits.text: The Genbaku Dome is the only building still standing near the hypocenter of the August 6, 1945 bomb—detonated at 8:15 in the morning just 160 meters away. Designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel and inaugurated in 1915 as the Hiroshima Prefectural Commercial Exhibition Hall, the building wasn't destroyed because the explosion's pressure came directly from above, and its vertical columns resisted the downward force. The city decided in 1966 to preserve it indefinitely as a memorial. Inscribed as a UNESCO site in 1996, it's not open to the interior—but from the banks of the Motoyasu, its skeleton of metal and burnt brick produces a striking effect.

The Peace Memorial Museum, at the other end of the park, opened in 1955. The 2019 renovation reoriented the exhibitions toward individual stories: personal effects of victims with their names, photos, and stories, a watch stopped at 8:15, a charred schoolboy's jacket. This is not an easy museum, but it's necessary. Allow at least 1.5 hours—audio guides are available in French.

At the center of Peace Memorial Park, the Cenotaph—a stone arch sheltering the names of all known victims—is aligned with the Flame of Peace (lit August 1, 1964, it will not be extinguished until all nuclear weapons have been eliminated) and the Dome, so that all three are visible in enfilade. Take time to walk through the park rather than in a straight line.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll along the Motoyasu—this river that borders the park was one of the only escape routes on August 6, 1945. Each August 6, hundreds of paper lanterns float on it at nightfall for the souls of the victims. Hiroshima is a resolutely lively city: try an okonomiyaki Hiroshima-style (layered in strata, very different from the Osaka version) in the Hondori covered arcades.

visits.text: Itsukushima Shrine, built in 593 then reconstructed in its current form in 1168 by Lord Taira no Kiyomori, is both a National Treasure and a UNESCO World Heritage site (since 1996). Its 56 vermilion wooden structures, connected by corridors totaling 275 meters, are built on stilts above the water so as not to 'defile' the sacred island. At high tide, the whole appears to float. The corridor floors have slightly spaced slats to let tidal water pass through without warping the structure. Check tide times before coming: the scene is radically different depending on water level.

The great torii of Itsukushima—16.6 meters high, 60 tons—is the current version built in 1875, the eighth in the shrine's history. It's made of camphor wood, chosen for its resistance to seawater, and stands upright solely by its own weight without cement. At low tide, you can walk to its base and touch the pillars. Tradition held that one should pass through it by boat to enter the shrine.

activities.text: The hike to the summit of Mount Misen (535 m), the island's sacred mountain, is the best way to see Miyajima beyond the shrine crowds. From the summit, the view over the Seto Inland Sea and its islands is extraordinary. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours ascending the forest trails, or take the ropeway to mid-height. In autumn, the island's red foliage makes it one of western Japan's most beautiful koyo spots.

Spending the night on the island is highly recommended—tour groups leave on the last afternoon ferry, and the island becomes peaceful. Very early in the morning, you'll have the shrine and the deer (hundreds roam freely, having done so for centuries) almost to yourself. The five-story pagoda of Senjokaku, built in 1587, merits a stop.

map_keywords: Kintai Bridge Iwakuni wooden bridge five arches

visits.text: Iwakuni's Kintaikyo Bridge is one of Japan's three famous bridges—built in 1673 by the region's third lord, Kikkawa Hiroyoshi, who sought to solve a recurring problem: floods of the Nishiki River regularly destroyed any ordinary bridge. The idea for five arches came to him from a Chinese painting depicting a bridge over West Lake in Hangzhou. It measures 193.3 meters long, 5 meters wide, and its three central arches rest on stone pillars without any tie rods—a feat of purely Japanese carpentry. The bridge you cross is the 1953 reconstruction, after a 1950 typhoon swept away the original that had stood for 277 years. Cross it in both directions to see the assembly technique beneath the arches.

activities.text: On the other side of the bridge, Kikko Park and the Yokoyama district preserve several Edo-period structures: two original samurai residences, the Shomeikan gate (1793), and the Kikkawa museums. In spring, thousands of cherry trees in the park make Kintaikyo one of the most beautiful hanami sites in Chugoku. A 3-minute ropeway ascends to Iwakuni Castle, rebuilt in 1962—the view of the bridge and valley from the summit is the day's best photo.

visits.text: Rurikoji Temple's five-story pagoda is one of Japan's National Treasures and one of the country's three most beautiful pagodas—built in 1442 in memory of Lord Ouchi Yoshihiro. Its 31.2 meters are covered in hinoki cypress bark in an elegant style that marries Japanese aesthetics with some continental Buddhist touches. Yamaguchi calls itself the 'Kyoto of the West'—under the Ouchi family in the 15th and 16th centuries, the city was a cultural center rivaling Kyoto, and Francis Xavier preached here in 1550.

The Akiyoshidai karst plateau, 45 minutes from Yamaguchi, is Japan's largest karst: 45 km² of grasslands dotted with white limestone rocks, remnants of coral reefs formed 300 million years ago. Below lie the Akiyoshido caves—with 10 km of known galleries, it's East Asia's largest cave. About 1 km of galleries is accessible to the public, with underground rivers, stalactites, and gigantic chambers.

activities.text: In the evening in Yamaguchi, the Yuda Onsen district offers street footbaths (ashiyu, free) and several traditional ryokans. Local legend tells that a white fox with injured paws came to heal in a natural spring—this is how Yuda's waters were supposedly discovered. The regional specialty is fugu (pufferfish) from Shimonoseki, 50 km away, which supplies the entire region.

visits.text: Motonosumi Shrine stands on the cliffs of Yamaguchi's north coast, facing the Sea of Japan. In 1955, a local fisherman dreamed that a white fox asked him to build a shrine on this promontory. The 123 vermilion torii that descend in a tunnel from the shrine to the cliff edge were erected progressively between 1987 and 1997. The contrast—brilliant red, cobalt sea, green cliff grasses—made the place world-famous, particularly after CNN ranked it among Japan's 31 most beautiful places in 2015. A unique feature: the offering box is fixed atop the first torii, 6 meters high. You must toss your coin so it falls inside—if it enters, your wish is granted. Arrive in the morning to avoid traffic jams on the narrow access road.

Tsunoshima Bridge connects the mainland to Tsunoshima Island over 1,780 meters above the Sea of Japan—it's one of Japan's longest free bridges to an island, opened in 2000. Driving on this slightly curved bridge, with the turquoise sea on both sides, is one of the country's most photogenic experiences. The island itself has white sand beaches and a small white lighthouse at the end of a pine-lined path.

activities.text: Just below Motonosumi Shrine, a fissure in the cliffs creates a striking natural phenomenon: the Ryugu no Shiofuki (the 'Dragon Palace's Spout'). Waves rush into the cavity and water sometimes shoots up to 30 meters high. The phenomenon is more spectacular in autumn and winter, during heavy seas. If you're lucky, a rainbow forms in the spray.

The coastal region around Nagato is also known for its terraced rice fields facing the sea—from the Yuya terrace, the stepped plots descend to the shore. In the evening, squid fishing boats illuminate the sea offshore. The nearest airport is Yamaguchi-Ube (about 1.5 hours drive)—plan accordingly for the return trip.

seo.h1_title: San'In and Hiroshima Road Trip: Japan's Secret Coast
seo.intro_paragraph: From Tottori to Nagato, this 10 days journey follows Japan's hidden face: the San'In coast along the Sea of Japan, punctuated by ancient shrines, mountain castles, and fishing ports forgotten by mainstream tourist circuits. From Izumo Taisha—the country's oldest shrine—to Hiroshima's Genbaku Dome, passing through the Adachi Garden ranked first in Japan for over 20 years, each stop blends deep history with pristine landscapes. A Japan far from the crowds, between the Sea of Japan and the Seto Inland Sea.
